en: Preface to the *Yinyi* (Explanations of Terms) for the *Dacheng* (Mahāyāna): Being of dull wit, I have the misfortune of being attached to the end of the Dharma-gate. Yet, regarding the commentaries of former sages, I have not at all perused them exhaustively.
Only the single commentary on the *Dacheng* composed by my teacher Ban did I ever open and read; I have never ceased from it even for a moment of eating or resting. Internally—

Regarding the purport of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, he analyzes it with meticulous detail, leaving no aspect of its meaning unaddressed. Compared to the various masters of antiquity, how could he be considered inferior?
Yet, when encountering ancient anecdotes within his work, there are instances where doubts remain unresolved, like attempting to untangle a complex knot with a wooden blade.
I fear that future scholars, having traveled a thousand li, might turn back at the ninety-ninth mile. Its...

Is this not truly a great pity? Being of dull wit, I have nevertheless sought out the classics and histories and consulted with men of profound virtue, desiring to compile a single collection of phonetic glosses to share with those of like mind.

Before long, however, I came to dwell in seclusion in the Western Mountains; my learning was superficial and my hearing scant, such that I did not dare to peer into the depths with the limited wisdom of a tube.
Thus, though I had the aspiration, I failed to achieve it. Recently, while traveling from the mountains to pay my respects to my spiritual teacher, I noticed [a work] upon his desk.
There exists a work titled *Dacheng yinyi* (Meanings and Pronunciations of the Mahāyāna). I asked, "Whose penmanship is this? Master Xin replied, "It is the penmanship of Dharma Master Xing.
The draft is finished, but it has not yet been entrusted to the carvers. There is one, Master Yi-yun, who oversees the publication of the *Dacheng*.
He wishes to contribute funds to have it printed at Jishan Hermitage so that it may circulate alongside the *Dacheng*. He once requested a preface from me, but due to my long illness..."
"I have not yet mastered it. Will you take its place? I replied, "Indeed, this is not something easily spoken of; it must wait until the scrolls are exhausted before it can be fully seen.

Within the Great Achievement (*Dacheng*), for all passages where the meaning is profound and subtle, or where ancient events are cited, I have provided thorough explanations and indirect analogies, as if pointing to the current to verify its source. I could not help but say with joy: "This..."
This is like the morning star appearing before the assembly of sincere scholars. Within this "Great Perfection" (Dacheng), all matters are fully provided for, leaving nothing to be desired.
From this day forward, those who contemplate the Great Perfection will surely see everything with a single glance.

Those who previously harbored frustrations or held lingering doubts will be like accumulated dust or frozen ice encountering the sun of wisdom and the breeze of compassion; there shall be nothing that is not dissolved and dispersed. Is this not so?
How excellent! It will cause those who are currently studying not to find the difficulties arduous, and those who have already studied to find their true delight.
Who would not say that this guidance by way of a swift and direct path is the very efficacy of phonology and semantics? Moreover, the subtlety of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* is beyond words;
yet when there is great accomplishment, it can be expressed through words. Great accomplishment draws upon many precedents from antiquity, and where there is phonology and semantics—

This can be clearly understood. Therefore, one knows that while the *Lotus Sūtra* (*Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*) is indispensable for achieving great accomplishment, the phonology and semantics (*śabdārtha*) are likewise indispensable for that great accomplishment.

Thus, these phonologies and semantics constitute the most essential element. How could they be neglected and left without transmission? Someone might say: "Phonology and semantics belong to the minor arts (*kṣudra-vidyā*).
How can they be considered appropriate for clarifying the principles of the scriptures? I replied: "Alas! If one regards phonology and semantics [in this way]..."

If one studies the minor [learning], how can the so-called major [learning] enter? It is like the principle that one who travels a long distance must not neglect the short steps, and one who ascends a height must not neglect the low ground.
How could one see the inner sanctum of the Lotus Sutra’s hall as being reached without first following the shallow and proximate paths of phonology and glossary?
I believe that phonology and glossary provide assistance toward the Great [Learning].
Completed. It is truly considered to be of benefit to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
Recorded respectfully by Jichong of Yanshan on the Buddha’s Day of the Jiashen year of the Kangxi era. *Fahua Dacheng Yinyi* (Phonology and Meaning of the Great Achievement of the Lotus Sutra).
Compiled by Jingsheng, a later scholar from Hedong.
The First of the Five Patriarchs of the Huayan School:
Master Dixin. Dixin is his title; his secular surname was Du, and his given name was Fashun. Those in the world who were deaf or mute, upon encountering him...

He was certainly able to hear and speak. Emperor Taizong of the Tang dynasty issued an edict, saying to him: "I am suffering from the heat of exhaustion. By what means can your divine power dispel it? The Master replied:
"Your Majesty’s sagely virtue governs the realm; why worry over a minor ailment? Simply issue a general amnesty, and Your Majesty’s person will naturally recover.

The Emperor followed his advice, and the illness was subsequently cured. Consequently, he was granted the title "The Emperor's Heart" (Dixin) and composed the *Dharmadhātu-dhyāna-mukha* (The Gate of Contemplation on the Dharma Realm).
2. Grand Master Yunhua. Yunhua is the name of a monastery; the Master resided in this temple, and thus it was named after him.
His surname was Zhao and his posthumous name was Zhiyan. He received the direct transmission from Emperor Taizong and passed it on to Xianshou.
His teachings were widely propagated. 3. Grand Master Xianshou. Xianshou is a posthumous title. His surname was Kang and his personal name was Fazang. His ancestors...
A man from the country of Kangju, by imperial decree of Empress Wu Zetian of the Tang dynasty, expounded the fundamental tenets of the *Avataṃsaka* at Taoyuan Temple.
A white light issued from his mouth and, in an instant, formed a canopy, causing the multitude of ten thousand people to cry out in joy.

He was summoned for an audience in the Changsheng Hall, where he pointed to a golden lion at the corner of the hall to illustrate the essence and function of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), thereby preaching the Dharma. Empress Wu attained realization; she subsequently composed [a work] concerning him.
This is titled *The Treatise on the Golden Lion*. Four: Master Qingliang. "Qingliang" is his style name. His surname was Xiathou, his given name was Chengguan, and he was a native of Kuaiji.
He composed the Great Commentary (*Da Shu*) on the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*. During the birthday festival of Emperor Dezong of the Tang dynasty, he was summoned to have an audience in the inner palace.
Because he was able to refresh the Emperor’s mind with the wondrous Dharma, he was subsequently granted the title "Qingliang. When Emperor Xianzong questioned him regarding the Avataṃsaka school...
The Emperor’s intent was profound, and [the Master] attained sudden enlightenment. He was further titled the State Preceptor Qingliang of the Great Tong.
He passed away in the third year of the Kaicheng era of Emperor Wenzong. In total, he served as the preceptor to seven emperors across nine reigns.
The nine reigns were those of Emperors Xuanzong, Suzong, Daizong, Dezong, Shunzong, Xianzong, Muzong, Jingzong, and Wenzong. The seven emperors were those from Daizong onwards.
[This was] the seventh [emperor]. Five. Grand Master Guifeng. Guifeng is an alternative name for Mount Zhongnan.
The Master resided on this mountain and thus acquired this title. His surname was He, his style name was Zongmi, and he was a native of Xichong in Guozhou.

Qingliang once said to him, "As for one who can follow me to traverse Vairocana’s Flower Treasury World, could it be you? Thereupon, he composed commentaries on the *Awakening of Faith*, the *Flower Ornament Sutra* (*Avataṃsaka*), and others.
In the *Pingdeng shuchao*, Emperor Wenzong of the Tang dynasty issued an edict inquiring about the general meaning of the Buddha-dharma and conferred upon him the title of Dade (Great Virtue).

During the reign of Emperor Xuanzong, he was posthumously honored with the title of Chan Master Dinghui (Master of Steadfast Wisdom). The details may be found in the *Qixin lun huiyue*. Here, I have extracted [the relevant passage] according to the *Sanzang fashu*.

In the *Analects*, it is said that Yan Yuan sighed deeply, saying: "The Master leads us on with such steady persistence and skillfully guides us. He broadens me with cultural learning and refines me with ritual propriety.

The commentary states: "Xunxun" describes a manner that is orderly and progressive; "yòu" means to lead forward and introduce. This refers to the broadening of knowledge through culture and the refinement of conduct through ritual.
This refers to the sequence of instruction. It means that although the Master’s Way is lofty and subtle, his teaching of others follows a sequential order.

This is like the various streams flowing toward the capital, as stated in the "Yugong" chapter of the *Shangshu*: "The Yangtze and Han rivers flow toward the sea as their capital. The commentary states: "Appearing [at court] in spring is called 'zhao' (audience); appearing in summer..."
It is called "the capital" (*zōng*). "The morning capital" (*cháo-zōng*) is the name for the feudal lords' audience with the Son of Heaven. The Yangtze and Han rivers converge at Jing;

though they are still far from the sea, the waterways are already settled and free from the calamities of blockages or breaches. Although they have not yet reached the sea, [they are as secure as if they had].
Yet their momentum has already surged toward the sea, like the feudal lords paying court to the Son of Heaven. [The character for "to see" (jiàn) is pronounced xiàn.
It resembles the stars surrounding the North Star;
as the *Analects* states: "The Master said: 'To govern by means of virtue is like the North Star, which remains in its place while the multitude of stars revolve around it.'"
The commentary states: "Zheng" (政) means "to rectify. It is that by which one rectifies the impropriety of others. "De" (德) means "attainment.
It refers to practicing the Way and thereby attaining realization within the mind. "Beichen" (北辰) is the North Pole; it is the pivot of Heaven.
It dwells in its place and does not move. "Gong" (共) means "to face toward. This describes how the myriad stars revolve around it from all four directions and turn toward it.
"Follow the old statutes. The *Shijing* says:

"Neither erring nor forgetting, one follows the old statutes. The commentary states: "Erring (*qiān*)" means to go astray; "following" (*shuài*) means to adhere to; "statutes" (*zhāng*) refers to the codes and laws.
That one's conduct does not deviate and nothing is forgotten is because one adheres to and employs the precedents of the past. — *The Book of Poetry*.
The chapter "Jiàlè" (Hypothetical Joy) in the *Dàyǎ* (Greater Odes) also appears in the "Lílóu" chapter of the *Mèngzǐ*. "Jià" (Hypothetical) is rendered as "jiā" (Exquisite) in the *Shī*.

Regarding the passage in the *Lúnyǔ*, "Yǒujiào wúlèi" (There is instruction, no categories), the Master said: "There is instruction, no categories. The commentary states: "Human nature is universally good, yet its categories include both good and evil."
The distinction between them is due to the taint of habitual tendencies. Therefore, when the gentleman provides instruction, all people can return to goodness;
one should not further debate the evil of their respective categories.
"Being good in succession and good in narration is the Middle Way. The Master said, "King Wu and the Duke of Zhou—were they not paragons of filial piety?

For filial piety consists in being good at continuing the will of one’s predecessors and good at narrating their deeds. The commentary states: "King Wu succeeded to the legacy of King Tai, King Ji, and King Wen..."
Because [the Duke of Zhou] possessed the empire, he perfected the virtues of Wen and Wu to honor his ancestors in accordance with their legacy;
this was the greatest instance of continuing one's will and carrying forward one's undertakings.
The Way of the King is broad and level; for a thousand ages its principles remain the same.
The Sovereign penetrates the Three Powers and presides over the myriad things. He transforms the world through non-action and bestows grace upon the people through the Way.
"Broad and level" means even and expansive. Being both even and expansive, who throughout the ages has not followed the same standard? See the *Hui-xuan-ji*.

The Brahma-sounds of Chu, Xia, Qin, and Luo are called Zhonghua (Central China), also termed Huaxia (Flourishing China) and Zhongxia (Central China). The regions of Huainan and Chu are not the central lands;
yet the tones and accents used for invocation in Chu and Luo vary in their lightness and heaviness. Now, the Sanskrit language of the Western Regions bears a resemblance to these. In the center—
Heaven is like the Central Plains; the other four continents are like Chu and Shu. See the *Huayan xuantan* (Profound Discussion on the Avataṃsaka).
The verse on the seventy-five dharmas states: "Eleven are matter-dharmas, one is mind-dharma, forty-six are mental concomitants, and fourteen are unconditioned."
The non-associated [factors] are three; the unconditioned factors are seventy-five, as seen in detail in the *Dharmasaṃkhyā*.
Regarding the twenty schools whose tenets differ, according to the *Samayabhedoparacanacakra*, more than one hundred years after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, Mā...
In the kingdom of Keta, at the city of Kusumapura, there reigned a king named Aśoka who governed Jambudvīpa.
Having received a single white parasol as a divine omen, his transformative influence harmonized both humans and spirits. At that time, the Sangha of the Buddha’s Dharma was first divided.

This occurred because the four assemblies—including the learned and virtuous elders from the borderlands such as Nāgasena—held differing views on five matters: impermanence, suffering, emptiness, non-self, and the tranquility of nirvana. Thus, they split.
They are divided into two schools: first, the Mahāsāṃghika; second, the Sthavira. From the Mahāsāṃghika, eight schools branched out, making nine schools in total:
first, the Mahāsāṃghika; second, the Ekavyāvahārika; third, the Lokottaravāda; fourth, the Gokulika; [and so forth].
5. The Bahulika (Many-Hearing) School; 6. The Prajñaptivāda (Proponents of Designation) School; 7. The Caitīya (Stūpa-Mountain) School; 8. The Aparaśaila (Western Mountain-Dwelling) School; 9.
The Uttaraśaila (Northern Mountain-Dwelling) School. From the Sthavira (Elder) School, two schools were divided: first, the Sarvāstivāda (Proponents of the Existence of All);
second, the Sthavira itself, which was subsequently renamed the Haimavata (Snowy-Mountain) School. From the Sarvāstivāda, nine schools were successively derived. Together—
The aforementioned two root schools form eleven branches: first, the Sarvāstivāda; second, the Haimavata;
third, the Vātsīputrīya; fourth, the Dharmottarīya; fifth, the Bhadrayānīya; sixth, the Saṃmitīya; and seventh, the Mahīśāsaka.

Eighth, the Mahīśāsaka school; ninth, the Dharmaguptaka school; tenth, the Kāśyapīya school; and eleventh, the Sautrāntika school. Together with the preceding nine schools, they constitute twenty schools.
See the *Bai fa ming men lun zui yan* (Supplementary Remarks on the *Śata-dharma-viśada-mukha-śāstra*).
The first stage is itself the eighth;
as the four-volume *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* says: "The first is then the eighth; the ninth is then the seventh; the seventh is likewise the eighth. The second is the third;
the fourth is the fifth; the third is the sixth. When there is nothing, what sequence can there be?"
The detailed meaning of these is found in the *Kojie* (Sectional Explanation).
Regarding the five dharmas, the three natures, the eight consciousnesses, and the two kinds of selflessness:

the five dharmas are called name (*nāman*), appearance (*nimitta*), conceptualization (*parikalpa*), correct wisdom (*samyagjñāna*), and suchness (*tathatā*). As for the three natures (*trisvabhāva*):

They are called dependent origination, conceptual construction, and accomplishment. As for the eight consciousnesses: the first five consciousnesses, the sixth mental consciousness, the seventh manas consciousness, and the eighth ālayavijñāna.
As for the two kinds of selflessness: the selflessness of persons and the selflessness of phenomena.
From the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*:

"Prediction" (*vyākaraṇa*) refers to the bestowal of a prediction regarding future attainment of Buddhahood, specifically the predictions concerning the eon, the land, and the name [of the Buddha]. Upon seeing the Great...
An Explanation of the Tibetan Pronunciation:
Carrying Hemp and Discarding Gold.
Once, there were three men who entered a mountain, each carrying a load of hemp. By chance, along the way, they saw countless bolts of cloth.
The wise man said, "I shall discard my load of hemp and take the cloth. The foolish man said, "I have traveled a long way carrying this;

it is merely a load of hemp, and we have not gone far yet. Furthermore, I see white silver ahead. The wise man discarded the cloth and took up the silver, while the foolish man continued as before to carry the hemp.
As they went further, he saw gold. The wise man discarded the silver and took up the gold, while the foolish man continued as before.

This burdening of hemp— this self-reliance on one's own views and refusal to follow others— is generally like this. [Recorded by] Li Shanlong upon seeing the *Miaoyin yi* (Explication of the Meaning of [Amitābha]).
During the Tang dynasty, Li Shanlong, a Left Gate Guard Commandant (zuò jiānmén xiào wèi), died suddenly during the Wǔdé era.
However, the area over his heart remained warm for the size of a palm; his family did not dare to enshroud him.

On the seventh day, he revived and recounted that at the time of his death, he was seized by the underworld authorities and brought to an office where several thousand prisoners were undergoing various punishments. An official led him...
When the mountain dragon arrived at the foot of the hall, a celestial official asked him, "What meritorious deeds did you perform while alive?
The dragon replied, "Whenever my fellow villagers established vegetarian feasts or gave lectures, I always contributed goods alongside them. The official asked, "What good karma did you perform?

The dragon replied, "I recited two fascicles of the Lotus Sūtra. The official said, "Excellent; you may ascend the steps. Once the mountain dragon had ascended, there was a high seat to the northeast.
The King said, "I request the Dharma Master to ascend the seat. Shanlong then took his place. As he opened the scripture, saying, "The Lotus Sutra, Chapter One:

Introduction," the King said, "I request the Dharma Master to stop. He descended from the seat and stood again at the foot of the steps. Looking into the hall, he found that not a single prisoner remained.
The King said to Shanlong, "The merit of your recitation of the sutra has benefited not only yourself, but has also caused these prisoners—"

The multitude all escaped their fates by hearing this sutra; how excellent is this! Details regarding other matters, such as traveling through various hells and finding them all empty through mindfulness of the Buddha, are not recorded here.
See the twentieth fascicle of the Fayuan zhulin (Pearl Forest of the Dharma Garden).

Shi Daoyu—also known as Yisu—constantly recited the *Lotus Sūtra* more than one thousand times. At the beginning of the Zhenguan era, as he was about to die from illness, he entrusted his friend Huikuo with these words:
"Although I have recited the sūtra until now, my hope has been for a spiritual response; yet at the moment of my death—"
"Later, there is no need to leave the remains exposed; bury them for ten years. When you come to exhume them, examine whether the root of the tongue has rotted away.
If it is found to be undecayed, erect a stupa for it to demonstrate the miraculous response to the scripture. Having finished speaking, he passed away. They buried him according to his instructions.
In the eleventh year of the Zhenguan era, Huikuo and a close friend went to the tomb and opened it. The flesh of the body had all vanished, yet only the tongue remained incorruptible. Thus it was.

Later, he erected a stupa for him. This is recorded in the eighteen fascicles of the *Fayuan zhulin* (Forest of Gems in the Garden of the Dharma) and also appears in the *Xu gaoseng zhuan* (Continued Biographies of Eminent Monks).
As for Yan Fahua, he was Yan Gong of Yangzhou during the Chen dynasty. He was originally a native of Quanzhou; because he had taken charge of his father’s [estate]...
He had inherited fifty thousand coins and went to Yangzhou to trade his goods. By chance, he saw a boat carrying turtles in the river and ransomed them for the fifty thousand coins.
While his parents were at home, they saw fifty people dressed in black arrive at their door at night to deliver money.
The coins were all slightly damp. Later, when Yan Gong returned home, his parents told him that the day the guests paid the money was the very day they had ransomed the soft-shelled turtles.
Thus, it was known that the fifty guests were all the turtles they had ransomed.

Subsequently, father and son took deep faith in the law of cause and effect and went together to Yangzhou to build a vihāra, where they dedicated themselves to copying the Lotus Sūtra; for this reason, he was named Yan Fahuā (Yan of the Lotus).
From the *Fayuan zhulin* (Forest of Gems in the Garden of the Dharma), Volume 18.

Regarding the nun Faxin of the Wu-de era of the Tang dynasty: There was a nun named Faxin in Hedong who constantly recited the *Lotus Sūtra*. She sought out a skilled calligrapher and prepared a pure chamber.
He transcribed the sutra, burning incense and perfuming his robes. Furthermore, he attached a bamboo tube to the sutra-copying room that led outside, allowing the scribe to exhale through it.
It took eight years to complete. When the monk Fadu of Longmen requested that he lecture on it, upon opening the scroll he saw only yellow paper with no characters at all.
He immediately sent it to a nun, who received it with tears of grief and washed the case with scented water.

They bathed themselves and wore [the scripture] upon their heads, circumambulating the Buddha and practicing the Way for seven days and seven nights. Upon opening it to inspect it later, the characters were as they had been before.
This is recorded in the twenty-seventh fascicle of the *Fayuan zhulin*. As for the case of the window-rooster listening to the Dharma, its feathers fell off spontaneously;

when it was transformed into a Dharma Master, he personally encountered Samantabhadra, who rubbed the crown of his head. Furthermore, there was the mountain ox that sniffed at the sutras while sitting in forgetfulness, wearing [the scripture] upon its head.
The shape of the horn. He was born as a high minister and was transformed by Mañjuśrī’s instruction; I shall not cite further details here.
Regarding the seven methods of establishing titles:

first, establishing a title based on a single person, such as the *Sūtra Spoken by the Buddha on Amitābha* and others. Second, establishing a title based on a single dharma, such as the *Mahā-...* [text truncated].

1. Titles established by means of general metaphors, such as the *Parinirvāṇa-sūtra* and others; 2. Titles established by means of specific metaphors, such as the *Brahmajāla-sūtra* and others; 3. Titles established by means of single metaphors, such as the *Brahmajāla-sūtra* and others; 4.

Titles established by means of persons and dharmas, such as the *Mañjuśrīparipṛcchā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra* and others; 5. Titles established by means of both dharmas and metaphors, such as the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and others.

Sixth, establishing the title by means of a metaphor, as in the *Tathāgata-siṃhanāda* and other sūtras. Seventh, establishing the title by means of its full descriptive attributes, as in the *Mahāvaipulya-buddhāvataṃsaka* and other sūtras.
See the *Jizhu sijiao yi* (Collected Annotations on the Ritual of the Four Teachings) and the *Sanzang fashu* (Numerical Categories of the Tripitaka).

The five hundred bhikṣus each spoke of the cause of the body, just as the five hundred bhikṣus had done. They asked Śāriputra, "Venerable One, regarding the cause of the body spoken of by the Buddha, what is it?
Śāriputra said, "Venerable sirs, you yourselves have each attained right liberation; you should know it for yourselves. For what reason [do you ask]?"

"Why do you ask such a question? A bhikṣu said, "Venerable sir, before I had attained right liberation, I thought that ignorance (*avidyā*) was the cause of the body. While practicing this contemplation, I attained the fruit of arhatship.
Another said, "Venerable sir, before I had attained right liberation, I thought that craving (*tṛṣṇā*) and ignorance were the causes of the body. While practicing..."

This was the time of his contemplation, when he attained the fruit of Arhatship. Some said that volitional formations (*saṃskāra*), consciousness (*vijñāna*), name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*), contact (*sparśa*), feeling (*vedanā*), craving (*tṛṣṇā*), grasping (*upādāna*), becoming (*bhava*), birth (*jāti*), food, and the five objects of desire (*pañcakāmaguṇa*) are the causes of the body.

At that time, after each of the five hundred bhikṣus had individually explained what they understood, they went together to where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him three times to the right, and paid their respects.
Having finished, they sat to one side and each spoke to the Buddha of the meaning of what they themselves had understood as described above.
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One, among these people, who is speaking correctly and who is not speaking correctly?
The Buddha told Śāriputra, "Excellent, excellent! Not a single one of these bhikṣus has spoken anything other than the correct teaching. [Excerpted from the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, Part 3]
Fifteen fascicles. Furthermore, there is the *Sūtra on Five Hundred Disciples Speaking of Their Own Past Origins*.
Second is the *Vimalakīrti Sūtra*, "The Chapter on Entering the Dharma-gate of Non-duality," which originally contained thirty-two bodhisattvas, each of whom spoke [of their realization].
Regarding the Gate of Non-dual Dharma, he later asked Mañjuśrī, "What is the entry into the gate of non-dual dharma?

Mañjuśrī replied, "According to my understanding, with respect to all phenomena, there is no speech and no discourse; there is no demonstration and no cognition; it is free from all questioning and answering."
"This is what it means to enter the gate of non-dual dharmas. Thereupon, Mañjuśrī asked Vimalakīrti, "We have each spoken for ourselves;
now, O Benevolent One, you should explain what constitutes entering the gate of non-dual dharmas. At that time, Vimalakīrti remained silent and spoke no word.
Mañjuśrī sighed in praise, saying: "Excellent, excellent! To be utterly devoid of words and speech—this is the true entry into the Dharma-gate of non-duality.
(The four-line response).

Regarding the fourfold correspondence between stimulus and response (*ganying*): first, a latent stimulus with a latent response; second, a latent stimulus with a manifest response; third, a manifest stimulus with a manifest response;
and fourth, a manifest stimulus with a latent response. What is their meaning? If, in the past, one has cultivated the three karmas (*trikarma*) well...
At present, although one has not yet set in motion the actions of body and speech, one relies upon the power of past goodness; this is called "dark potential" (*mingji*).
Although no manifest spiritual response is seen, one is secretly benefited by the Dharma-body. Without seeing or hearing, one awakens and knows; this is what is meant by "dark benefit.
Second, regarding dark potential and manifest benefit: having planted goodness in the past, the dark potential is already established, and one thus encounters a Buddha.

Hearing the Dharma and obtaining benefit in the present constitutes what is called "manifest benefit. This refers, for example, to those who were the very first to attain liberation when the Buddha first appeared in the world;
they had never practiced in the present life, yet the Buddhas, perceiving their latent capacities from past lives, went of their own accord to deliver them—this is precisely that meaning.

Third, regarding the manifestation of capacity and the manifestation of response: though one’s current body and speech are diligent and unremitting, they are able to evoke a descent [of the Buddha], as follows:

When Sudatta knelt for a long time, the Buddha went to Jetavana. When Candracchattra bowed his body, the Sage stood at the threshold of the gate. These cases are like those who immediately practice repentance at a place of enlightenment;
they are able to evoke spiritual auspicious signs, which constitutes a manifest capacity meeting with a manifest response. Fourth, regarding a manifest capacity meeting with a hidden response:

it is like a person who, though diligent and suffering throughout a lifetime, accumulates a thick store of present goodness that does not manifest as a response, yet possesses its benefit in a hidden manner.
This explains the subtle benefit for those with karmic affinity. For a detailed examination, see the sixth fascicle of the *Fahua Xuan Yi* (Profound Meaning of the Lotus Sutra).
Regarding the thirty-six phrases of response and resonance:
previously, the subtle and manifest were discussed interchangeably, briefly citing four phrases; if one were to distinguish them fully:

This takes the four capacities (*mī*) as its foundation: namely, the hidden capacity (*miṅ jī*), the manifest capacity (*xiǎn jī*), the capacity that is both hidden and manifest (*yì míng yì xiǎn jī*), and the capacity that is neither hidden nor manifest (*fēi míng fēi xiǎn jī*).
The hidden refers to the past; the manifest refers to the present; the hidden-and-manifest refers to the past and present; and the neither-hidden-nor-manifest refers to the future.

The "Gaozi" chapter of Mencius. *Héng* (衡) is the same as *héng* (橫).

Regarding the contemplation of one's wife and concubines as being like painted vases, the *Udānavarga* (Chuyao jing) states: Long ago, there was a man of licentious character whose mind was solely intent on female beauty, and he could not part from them.

Later, when he was informed exactly as she had said, her husband felt profound shame and remorse.
He reflected within himself, "I wonder if I am truly a *srotāpanna*? Thereupon, he immediately ceased his sexual desires.

His wife asked her husband, "For what reason have you permanently ceased your sexual activities? Her husband then painted a beautiful jar, filled it with excrement and filth, and secured its mouth with a tight lid.
He ordered his wife to embrace it, saying, "It is no different from me. Following his instructions, the wife embraced the jar and would not let go. Her husband—
He broke the jar and said to his wife, "Why do you embrace this broken jar? The wife replied, "It is not so.
Her husband said, "I observe your body; it is even more wretched than this jar. From head to foot, among these thirty-six constituent parts, what is there to be craved?"

"Eating parched grain and eating herbs"—Mencius said, "When Shun ate parched grain and herbs, it was as if he would do so for the rest of his life. The commentary states: "Fàn" means "to eat."

*Qiù* refers to parched grain; *rú* also refers to food. This means that the mind of the sage does not harbor longings for external things because of poverty or low status, nor does it undergo internal agitation because of wealth or honor.
He remains at peace with whatever he encounters, as nothing is preoccupied by his own self; this is because the nature and lot allotted to him are fixed.

This means to engage its pivotal mechanism and strike at its essential joints. See the *Baohun yinyi* (Explanations of Words and Meanings of the Precious Instructions).

Regarding the analogy drawn from what is near, the *Lunyu* states: "The Master said: 'To be able to draw analogies from what is near may be called the method of benevolence (*ren*). The commentary notes: 'Analogies (*pi*) are metaphors (*yu*').**" *(Note: The asterisks indicate that the original Chinese text contains a quotation from the Analects with its corresponding commentary.)*
This is a method. By drawing near upon one's own person, one uses what one desires for oneself as an analogy for others; thus, one knows that their desires are likewise the same.

When Master Zhuang was escorting a funeral procession, he passed by the tomb of Huizi. He turned to his attendants and said, "In the city of Ying, there was a man who had plaster smeared on the tip of his nose until it was as thin as a fly's wing.
He asked the artisan Shi to chisel it away. As Shi brandished his adze with such speed that it created a wind, he listened carefully and struck; the plaster was completely removed."
The plaster was applied and his nose was not injured; the man of Ying stood there without losing his composure.
When Lord Yuan of Song heard of this, he summoned the artisan Shi and said, "Try, for my sake, to chip away at it. The artisan Shi replied, "I was indeed able to do so in the past.
However, my 'raw material' died long ago. Since the death of that master, I have had no material to work upon, nor anyone with whom to converse."
This is from the "Miscellaneous Chapters" of the *Zhuangzi*. Regarding the "Goose and the Pearl":
Once, there was a bhikṣu begging for alms who arrived at the house of a pearl-maker. He happened to find the artisan working on behalf of a king to pierce a pearl. Upon seeing the bhikṣu...

The Bhikṣu came, joyfully holding his alms-bowl, entering the house to receive food. The Bhikṣu’s robe was crimson; as the sun shone upon it, light was produced, and its reflection cast upon the precious pearl made it appear the same color—crimson.
A goose standing nearby, thinking it was meat, swallowed it. The Bhikṣu saw this, but could not reach it in time to protect it.
A jeweler, carrying a bowl filled with food, arrived and offered it to the Bhikṣu. They exchanged thanks and departed. That man...
Later, he discovered that one pearl was missing and suspected that the bhikṣu had stolen it.

He immediately pursued and seized him, returning with him to reprimand him, saying, "Since you are a son of the Śākya, how can you lack integrity and shame to steal my royal pearls? The bhikṣu replied, "I have done no such thing. The man thought to himself in secret:
"If he were not treated with harsh discipline, the jewel could not be recovered. He then subjected him to flogging until blood flowed from every part of his body. A goose came to lick the blood;
the man, filled with rage, struck it with a staff, and the goose died as a result. The bhikṣu then requested to see whether the goose was dead or alive.
He replied, "It is already dead. The bhikṣu said, "A goose swallowed your pearl. The man did not believe him. The bhikṣu said, "I truly saw it swallow it.
He then took a knife and cut open the goose's belly; indeed, he found the pearl. The man felt ashamed and apologized, saying, "Why did you not show me sooner?
You have made me blind and foolish, causing your venerable body to suffer such pain as I committed this evil deed. The bhikṣu—

He said: "I have received the prohibitive precepts; I would rather sacrifice my own body and life than harm an ant's egg. If I had shown [the way] to you beforehand, I would surely have caused the death of that goose.
How can one who does not protect sentient beings be called a holder of the precepts? This is from the *Vibhāṣā-śāstra* and the *Mahāvyūha-śāstra*.
There were some bhikṣus traveling through a wilderness who were plundered by bandits. Fearing the bhikṣus, the bandits went to inform the village and intended to kill them all.
One among the bandits had previously been a renunciant; he said to his companions, "The dharma of the bhikṣus..."
He was not permitted to harm the grass, so he tied himself with it; in the end, he could not go on. He then tied himself with the grass and left him there before departing.
The bhikṣus, fearing they might harm the life-force of the grass, did not dare to move. At that time, the king was hunting;
seeing them, he asked, "By what cause and condition are you tied to the grass and unable to move? The bhikṣus replied, "The Buddha has taught that grass and trees are spirits."
The village [inhabitants] did not move because they revered the Buddha’s words. The king, acting as a bhikṣu, untied their straw bonds before departing.
This is from the sixth fascicle of the *Avadāna-śataka* (Piyuyi jing), and is also seen in the *Mahāvyūha-śāstra* (Dazhuangyan lun) and the *Fayuan zhulin*.
*Analects*: "If one cannot be patient with small matters, one will bring disorder to great plans.

*Jie* refers to the bracket-sets atop the columns. *Zao* is the name for an aquatic plant. *Zhue* refers to the short pillars atop the beams. It was intended to be a chamber for housing tortoises;
thus, mountain patterns were carved upon the *jie* and designs of *zao* plants were painted upon the *zhue*. At that time, people considered Wen Zhong to be wise. Confucius said:

In the art of architectural splendor, when Jin Xian Wenzi completed his new residence, the Great Officers of Jin went there to congratulate him. Zhang Lao said, "How magnificent its height!

"Also. Huàn. Huànlàn means 'abundant and flourishing. It appears in the *Liji*, *Tangong Xia*. [The text continues:

*Yourán* (glistening) describes the abundance of the clouds; *pàirán* (pouring down) describes the abundance of the rain; *bórán* (suddenly emerging) describes the manner of their growth. This passage is from the *Mencius*.

The *Huangliang Yimeng Yiwenzhi* (Strange Tales of the Yellow Millet Dream): While Lü Wēng was traveling on the road through Handān, he came upon an inn where a young man named Lú Shēng was lamenting his poverty.
Having finished speaking, he fell asleep. Just as the host was cooking yellow millet, the old man reached into his bag, took out a pillow, and gave it to the youth.

The man said, "Rest your head upon this, and your fortunes shall be as you wish. Wang Chih placed his head upon it and dreamed that he reached a kingdom where his fame and office brought him fulfillment;

he experienced wealth and nobility for over fifty years before growing old and sickly, passing away. He stretched himself awake to find Lü Wong standing beside him, while the host was still cooking yellow millet porridge that had not yet been finished.
Wang Chih thanked him, saying, "It was by means of this, sir, that you stilled my desires."
In the seventh day of the fifth year of the Yongping era of the Han dynasty, Liu Chen and Ruan Zhao of Shan County entered Mount Tiantai together. They became lost and could not find their way back.
Looking far off at the mountain, they saw a peach tree with many ripe fruits; they climbed up by grasping the vines and each ate several of them.

Descending the mountain again, they took their cups and went to fetch water at the edge of a stream. There were two women there who, upon seeing them, laughed and said, "Liu and Ruan, you two brothers, why have you come so late?
They then invited them into a cavern where they partook of wine, meat, and music, eventually becoming husband and wife.

When they returned home, no one recognized them; however, they learned that their seventh-generation descendants still existed, for it was passed down that their ancestors had entered the mountains long ago and lost their way.

He was able to return. In the eighth year of the Taiyuan era of the Jin dynasty, he departed once more, and it is unknown where he went. Master Hanshan’s commentary states: "Though the form is transformed, the nature remains constant, like fire persisting when the fuel is exhausted.

There is a transmission of dharma through forms, like the passing of fire from one piece of wood to another; thus, it is born again and again without ceasing, transforming and renewing itself without end.
Therefore, it is like the transmission of fire from fuel, such that its exhaustion is not known. Master Yuyin’s commentary states: "Its..."
That which can be exhausted is the firewood; that which cannot be exhausted is the fire. That which has an end is the physical form; that which is inexhaustible is the spirit.
The firewood has an end, but the fire is infinite; the form has an end, but the spirit does not perish.

The Great Master Huìsī of Nanyuè was surnamed Lǐ and was a native of Wǔjīn. He frequently dreamed of a foreign monk who exhorted him to leave secular life; he subsequently took leave of his kin to enter the Way.
From Mount Dasu in Gwangju, he proceeded directly to Nanyue. His disciples were very numerous, and the Master was troubled by a lack of water.
Suddenly, he saw moisture beneath a cliff; he struck it with his monk’s staff, and indeed found a spring. Yet, as it was not yet sufficient for all, two tigers led the Master up the ridge.
They roared and pawed at the spring—this is the present-day Tiger-Paw Spring (Hupao Quan). Furthermore, he discovered human remains beneath a rock, and subsequently...
Thereupon, a stupa was built; this is the present-day Stupa of the Three Lives (*Sengsheng*). The Master frequently lectured on the *Prajñāpāramitā* for the assembly;

this site corresponds precisely to the central point of Mount Nanyue, which is the present-day Prajñā Monastery. Because Master Zhi had delivered a prophetic message, saying: "Why do you not descend the mountain to transform sentient beings?
What is the use of gazing at the Milky Way? the Master replied: "The Buddhas of the three periods of time are all swallowed by me in a single mouth."
Having swallowed [all] up, what further sentient beings are there to convert? Since the wind of his teaching flourished, his fame was heard everywhere.

At the end of his life, he passed away peacefully. The details may be found in the *Continued Biographies of Eminent Monks* (*Xu gaoseng zhuan*) and the *Biographies of Divine Monks* (*Shen seng zhuan*).

He looked back repeatedly as he departed.

Regarding the line "The yellow liquid does not pour into an earthen jar," the *Shi Jing* says: "Resplendent is the jade libation cup; the yellow liquid is within it. Upon the gentle and easy nobleman, blessings and emoluments descend. The commentary states:

This is an *xing* (an exclamation of joy). *Se*: the appearance of being fine and dense. *Yu-zan*: the *gui-zan* (jade ladle). It has a *gui* (sacrificial jade tablet) as its handle, with gold for the scoop, green metal for the exterior, and vermilion in the center.

*Huang-liu* (yellow flowing liquid): this is the *yu-chang* (fragrant libation). One brews it from *ju-shu* (black millet) to make wine, then mixes in ground *yu-jin* (turmeric) and boils it together so that it is fragrant and pervasive.
One uses the *zan* to draw and pour it for the *guo* (consecration ritual). This refers to the descent [of the spirits].
This is the conclusion. When one speaks of the jade libation cup (*yuzhen*) that is *se* (resplendent), there must be the "yellow flow" (*huangliu*) within it;

when one speaks of the noble person who is serene and joyful (*qiaodi*), there must be blessings and emolument descending upon their person. It is clear that precious vessels are not presented with vulgar food, nor is the yellow flow poured into earthenware jars.
Thus we know that those of great virtue must enjoy fortune and longevity, whereas blessings and grace do not descend upon those who lack such merit.
"This is a lewd person. This is from the "Wen Wang" chapter of the *Dà yǎ*.

Chaos died daily.

T’ao and Hu met by chance in the land of Chaos, and Chaos treated them with great kindness. T’ao and Hu plotted together.
To repay the virtue of the Chaos, [Fenghou] said: "All people possess seven apertures for seeing, hearing, eating, and breathing, yet this being alone lacks them.
Let me try boring them. He bored one aperture per day; on the seventh day, the Chaos died. This is from the *Inner Chapters* of the *Zhuangzi*.
Mencius said: "Yangzi adopts the doctrine of 'selfishness' (wei-wo). He would not pluck out a single hair from his body to benefit the world. The commentary states:
Yangzi’s name was Zhu. "Taking" (qu) conveys the sense of mere sufficiency. To take for oneself means merely to be sufficient for oneself, without extending to others.
Regarding the yellow leaves used to stop a child’s crying: when an infant is weeping, the parents take yellow leaves from a willow tree and say to him, "Do not cry, do not cry;
I will give you gold. Upon seeing this, the infant conceives the notion that they are real gold and immediately stops crying. This is from the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*.
In the twentieth fascicle of the *Pán jīng* (Discourse on Turning Over), citing the *Lúnyǔ* three times, it says:

"Then he did not repeat it. The commentary states: "Fèn" (憤) refers to the state of mind seeking penetration but not yet attaining it;
"fěi" (悱) refers to the appearance of wishing to speak with the mouth but being unable to do so. "Qǐ" (啟) means to open up his understanding; "fā" (發) means to bring forth his expression.
Regarding objects that have four corners, by lifting one, one can know the other three. "Fǎn" (反) has the meaning of returning to provide mutual verification; "fù" (復) means to inform again.
It is so. Acting upon the shadow of the whip:

when a non-Buddhist asked the World-Honored One, "I do not ask for words regarding existence, nor do I ask for words regarding non-existence," the World-Honored One remained silent for a long while. The non-Buddhist...

He prostrated himself and departed. Ānanda asked the Buddha, "What principle did the outsider realize that he praised you and then left?
The World-Honored One replied, "It is like a fine horse that, upon seeing the shadow of the whip, immediately gallops forward. (See *Zongmen tongyao*, *Wudeng huiyuan*, and *Zhuyuelu*).

The *Gāthā-bhaiṣajya-avaivarta-sūtra* states: "When sentient beings see the agada medicine, all their illnesses are completely eliminated. This is translated as "Universally Removing" (*pǔqù*), because it can remove all diseases.
It is also rendered as "Perfectly Responsive" (*yuán yìng*). See the *Mingyiji*. Furthermore, "a-ga-da" (agada) means "universal" (*pǔ*) here.
*Gāthā*. This is translated as "to go away. It means that for one who takes this medicine, all diseases within the body are universally eliminated.

It is also said that *a* means "no" and *gāthā* means "disease"; having taken this medicine, there will be no further disease. See the *Huayan jing yinyi* (Phonetic and Semantic Commentary on the Avataṃsaka Sūtra).

"To awaken these people with this Way"—this was what Mencius recounted from the words of Yi Yin: "When Heaven brought forth these people, it caused those who knew first to awaken those who know later, and those who were enlightened first to awaken those who are enlightened later.
I am one among the people of Heaven who has been enlightened first; I shall use this Way..."
"To awaken the people; if not I who shall awaken them? (From the section on Mencius). Regarding the "Poisonous Drum," the *Guǎngzhì* states:
"The *hèndú* (poisonous fowl) is as large as a hawk, with a neck eight inches long and purple-green plumage covering its entire body."
This is a poison that feeds upon snakes and vipers. The male is named Huī and the female is named Yīn. If its feathers and plumage are used to sprinkle wine, one dies as soon as it touches the lips;
rhinoceros horn is used to counteract it. This was the case in the past when Wang Mang administered poisoned wine to Emperor Ping.

When it ascends into the air, the sun and moon lose their luster; when it falls to the ground, all plants and trees wither. If people see it, their eyes go blind and their bodies break out in sores; those who encounter its shadow lose consciousness.
When one dies, after death, blood is smeared upon a drum; anyone who hears its sound will surely die. Only the "Resurrecting Soul Incense" (fanhun xiang) can save them.
Thus, the Junior Preceptor Tiandong said in a small assembly: "Having fully obtained the Resurrecting Soul Incense, they come equally to strike the Poison-Smeared Drum.
In the first year of the Yanyan era of the Han dynasty, an envoy from the Yuezhi Kingdom of the Western Regions was sent to present this incense as an offering.

It weighed four *liang* and was as large as a sparrow’s egg, with a color like that of a mulberry fruit. In the first year of the Shih era, a great epidemic broke out in the capital, and those who died accounted for more than half the population.
The Emperor took the incense and burned it; those who had been dead for less than three days all returned to life. The fragrance did not cease for three months.

The incense originates from Mount Ren-niao on the continent of Juku-zhou. Its trees resemble maple; their fragrance can be smelled for several *li*. They are called the "Resurrecting Soul Tree" (*fanhun shu*).

When its roots are felled and boiled in five cauldrons, the resulting liquid is black and viscous. It has three names: first, "Startling the Vital Spirit" (*jing jinghun*); second, "Returning to Life" (*fansheng*); third, "Vibrant Sandalwood" (*zhentan*).
The four names for the kalpa of death are found in the *Shiyi zhuan*.
When a gentleman loves others, he does so through virtue:
when Zengzi was bedridden with illness, Yue Zhengzichun sat at the foot of the bed, while Zeng Yuan and Zeng Shen sat at his feet.
A youth sat in a corner holding a candle. The youth said, "It is so ornate and bright; is this the bedstead of a Great Officer? Zichun said, "Stop.
When Zengzi heard this, he looked startled and called out, "Ah! Is it so ornate and bright? Is this the bedstead of a Great Officer?
Zengzi replied, "Indeed, this was a gift from Ji Sun. I have not yet been able to replace it. Rise up, my boy, let us change the bedstead. Zengzi then rose.
Yuan said, "The Master’s illness has become critical; it cannot be changed. Fortunately, he has reached the dawn; I beg you to respectfully change his bedding.
Zengzi said, "Your love for me is not as that of the other. A gentleman loves others through virtue."
"The petty man loves others with mere expediency. What do I seek? It is enough for me that I die upright.
He was lifted up, supported, and moved to a new seat; before he had even settled back upon it, he passed away. (From the *Tán Gōng* chapter of the *Lǐjì*).
"The land of Sangjian Puchang and the music of Sangjian Puchang are the music of a ruined state. The commentary states: "Sangjian Puchang refers to the region of Wei;
it is the area between the Sang Forest and along the Puchang River. The *Shiji* records that when Duke Ling of Wei was visiting Jin, he halted at Puchang one night.

Upon hearing the sound of the lute, he summoned Shi Juan to listen to it and transcribe it. When the state of Jin came to command Juan to perform it for Duke Ping, Shi Kuang said, "This is the seductive music of Shi Yan.
When King Wu campaigned against Zhou, Shi Yan threw himself into the Pu River and died.
Therefore, if one hears this sound, it must be upon the banks of the Pu River. This is excerpted from the "Record of Music" chapter of the *Book of Rites*.
One does not consider the prevention of a fire by bending the chimney.
During the reign of Emperor Xuan of the Han dynasty, the Huo family was initially extravagant. Xu Fu of Maoling submitted a memorial stating that they should be restrained in a timely manner.
Later, when the Huo clan was executed and exterminated, all those who had reported them were enfeoffed. People said of Xu Fu’s petition: "I, your servant..."
A guest passing by a host’s house observed that the hearth was directly facing the chimney and that firewood was piled nearby.

The guest said to the host, "You should have the chimney rebuilt so it is curved and move the wood further away; otherwise, you will surely suffer a great calamity. The host did not heed his words. Shortly thereafter, the house indeed caught fire.
The neighbors joined together to extinguish it, and fortunately, the flames were brought under control. Thereupon, the host slaughtered an ox and prepared wine to express his gratitude to the guest.

The neighbors sat down; those who had been burned and scalded sat at the top, while the others each took their places according to the rank of their merit. However, the man who had warned of the curved roof was not recorded among them. A person said to the host:
"If you had listened to the guest's words earlier, you would not have wasted oxen and wine, and in the end there would have been no disaster from fire.

Now, when discussing merits and requesting rewards, the one who bent the roof and moved the firewood receives no favor, while those with scorched heads and burnt faces are treated as guests of honor? The host...
When people wake up, they seek counsel; now Xu Fu of Maoling has repeatedly submitted memorials stating that the Huo clan poses a threat and that measures must be taken to prevent it.

Had Fu’s words been followed, the state would not have incurred the expense of granting fiefs and noble ranks, nor would ministers have suffered the calamity of being accused of rebellion and exterminated.
Since those past events are already concluded, yet Fu alone has not received the credit for them, may Your Majesty examine this.
He valued the strategy of moving the firewood and bending the chimney over those who had scorched their hair and suffered burns, placing them to the right [in honor].

The Emperor subsequently bestowed ten rolls of ceremonial silk upon him, and he was later promoted to the rank of Lang (Court Gentleman). This is recorded in the *Biography of Huo Guang* and the *Comprehensive Mirror for Aid in Government*.
It is like beating a drum while searching for a lost child.
Laozi said to Confucius, "Master, you have already reached the goal by acting in accordance with virtue and proceeding along the Way."
"And yet, why does he repeatedly proclaim benevolence and righteousness? It is like beating a drum while searching for a runaway son.
Alas! Master [Confucius] confuses the nature of man. The *Jingjie* (Essential Explanation) says: "Jiejie" describes the appearance of laborious exertion. A "runaway son" is a son who has fled;
to search for him by beating a drum is to hasten his disappearance. Likewise, to govern the world by proclaiming benevolence and righteousness is to hasten its disorder.
This is from the "Tian Dao" chapter of the *Zhuangzi*. Regarding the lament of Zhongni (Confucius) concerning floating upon the sea, the *Lunyu* records:
"The Master said, 'If the Way cannot be practiced, I shall mount a raft and float upon the sea. Chengzi (Cheng Yi) commented: "The lament of floating upon the sea expresses grief."
That the world lacks a worthy ruler is like adding a foot to a snake. [This is recorded in] the *Shizi*.
Chen Zhen saw the Bearer of the Seal of Chu, Zhao Yang, and said: "There was a man who gave a cup of wine to his fellow officers. The officers..."
He said, "Let us draw snakes on the ground; whoever finishes first shall drink alone. One man finished first, raised his cup, and said, "I can add feet to it.
As he was adding the feet, the other man snatched the wine and drank, saying, "A snake has no feet.
Now that you have added them, it is no longer a snake."
*Fahua Dacheng Yinyi*, Scroll Three.

For thirty years, I have used my mind to conjecture about the Chan Master Zhenneng of Jingzhu Monastery in Hangzhou. He studied under Jinshan Daguan Ying, and subsequently asked him: [The text continues with the dialogue.]

"Your disciple has a superficial understanding of the sutras and treatises, yet I have no faith in Chan at all. I pray that the Master will resolve my doubts. Guanding said, "Since you do not believe in Chan, how can you claim to understand the sutras?
Chan is the mainstay of the sutras, and the sutras are the net of Chan. Grasp the mainstay to straighten the net; only then will you fully realize Chan and see the sutras."
The Master said, "I shall explain Zen for you. Guanzhi said, "The subsequent text is long. The Master said, "If it is so, then the Sūtras and Zen are of one essence.
Guanzhi said, "The Buddha and the Patriarchs do not have two minds; it is like a hand forming a fist, or a fist opening into a hand.
Because of this, the Master attained realization and composed a verse: "For thirty years I have used my mind to speculate... (and so forth). [This account is recorded in] *The Five Lamps*.
Huìyuán: "To avoid injuring the blade or offending the hand.

Master Hámàn (Zhǎngfú) states in his *Commentary on the 'Nourishing the Lord of Life' Chapter* of the *Inner Chapters of Zhuāngzǐ*: "Allowing the blade to glide freely, there is still room for surplus."
What harm is there in wounding one's edge or injuring one's hand?
When Śāriputra was a brahmin begging for his eyes, he practiced the bodhisattva path for sixty kalpas; at that time, there was a person who begged for his eyes. Śāriputra...
Śāriputra said, "The eye has no fixed abode; why do you seek it? If you require my body or my possessions, I shall give them to you.
The beggar replied, "I only wish to have the eyes. Śāriputra then plucked out one eye and gave it to him.
Having received the eye, the beggar spat upon it and trampled it with his foot. Śāriputra said, "People such as these are difficult to save; it would be better not to [save them]."
Tiao. Having long since subdued the cycle of birth and death, he thereupon turned his merit toward the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*).

Upon reading the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* (Chidu lun), he encountered the passage where Wang Sun Yu, the Grand Master of Chu, answers Zhao Jianzi. When Wang Sun Yu was on a diplomatic mission to Jin, Duke Ding hosted him. Zhao Jianzi accompanied the ceremony with the clashing of jade pendants and questioned Wang Sun Yu.
Sun Yu said, "Does the white jade pendant of Chu still remain? He replied, "Indeed, it does. Lord Jian asked, "How long has it been considered a treasure?

Sun Yu said, "It has never been considered a treasure. What Chu treasures are Guanshefu, who is able to compose instructive rhetoric to conduct affairs among the feudal lords, ensuring that our ruler is not made a subject of idle gossip; and there is also Zuo Shi Yixie..."

He possesses the capacity to expound the canonical teachings and thereby categorize the myriad things; he presents reports of successes and failures to our humble lord morning and evening, ensuring that our lord does not forget the legacy of the former kings.
Furthermore, he can bring joy to the spirits above and below, and harmonize their desires and aversions with the Way.
To ensure that the spirits have no resentment or suffering within the state of Chu—this is the true treasure of Chu. As for the white jade pendant, it was merely a plaything of the former kings;
what treasure is it? The details of this may be found in the *Guoyu*.

The *Gāndhārī* poem says: "The stalwart warrior, the public lord’s bulwark. The commentary states: "Fūfū" describes the appearance of martial vigor; "gān" refers to a shield. Both the gān (shield) and the city serve to ward off the outside and protect the inside.

This is from the "Zhōu Nán" section of the *Guófēng* in the *Shījīng*. (*Zuǒ*) (Note: The term *gāndhārī* here is likely a transcription error or a specific transliteration of a Sanskrit term related to the source text; it is rendered as such to preserve the original character.)
The *Biographies* (Zhuan) state: "When the Way prevails in the world, princes and lords can serve as shields and bulwarks for the people.

The *Sutra of the Flower Garland* (*Avataṃsaka-sūtra*) states: "On the Snowy Mountains there is a medicine named 'Good Vision' (*Sudarśana*). Seeing, hearing, smelling, or touching it eliminates all ailments."

Regarding the ram butting against the fence, the *Book of Changes* (*Zhouyi*) states: "The ram butts against the fence; it can neither retreat nor advance. The commentary notes: "Its vigor has reached its limit and its movement is at its extreme;
thus it butts the fence and cannot retreat. Yet, because its nature is fundamentally supple, it is likewise unable to carry its progress forward."

"Having no words to be chosen [for rejection] from one's mouth. The *Classic of Filial Piety* says: "One does not speak what is not in accordance with the Law; one does not act what is not in accordance with the Way.

Having no words to be chosen from one's mouth and no conduct to be chosen from one's body, one's words fill the world without verbal faults, and one's conduct fills the world without resentment or malice. The commentary states: "All that is spoken conforms to the Law."
When one has attained deliverance, there are no words from the mouth that require selection; though speech may fill the world, it will not result in verbal transgression.
When all that is practiced accords with the Way, there are no actions of the body that require selection.
Although one may travel throughout the world, one will not incur the resentment or hatred of others.

Regarding the terms "left-diao" (left-fur) and "right-inserted," the *Shuowen Jiezi* states that the *diao* is a species of marmot, large and yellowish-black in color, originating from the Hu Dingling country; another account says it originates from the tribes of the northeast.

*Gujin zhu* (Notes on Antiquity and the Present): "The crown of the Zhongshu Shizhong is adorned with *diao* (sable). Xu Guang says: 'In the north, it is cold; [people] use *diao* fur to warm their foreheads. This was attached to the crown and thus became a head ornament.

*Hanguanyi* (Rituals of Han Officials): Regarding the *diao-chan* (sable-cicada), Ying Shao says: "'Gold' is taken for its hardness and strength; the 'cicada' is taken for its high perching and pure drinking;
the *diao* is taken for its inner toughness and vigor and outer warmth and glossiness. *Han Huanzhe zhuan* (Biographies of Eunuchs of the Han): Qin... [text fragment].
The Han *zhongchangshi* (Palace Attendants) were recruited from both eunuchs and scholar-officials; their caps were adorned with silver rings and left-pointing sable fur (*zhuāo*).
Emperor Ming changed these to gold rings and right-pointing sable fur, and appointed exclusively eunuchs to these positions.
The King said to Yanmei A-heng: "You must instruct my will. You are like the malt and yeast in making sweet wine; you are like the salt and plum in making harmonious soup.
The commentary states: "Wine is not made without malt and yeast; soup is not made harmonious without salt and plum. Thus it is with the ruler..."
Though one possesses excellent natural qualities, it is only through the guidance of worthy men that one can perfect virtue.
In making wine, if the malt is too much, it will be too bitter; if the yeast is too much, it will be too sweet. Only when the malt and yeast are in balance is the wine perfected.

In making soup, if the salt is excessive, it will be too salty; if the plums are excessive, it will be too sour. Only when the salt and plums are in balance is the soup perfected. A minister’s relation to his ruler should be likewise.
"The supple complements the firm; it can rescue what is blocked. From left and right, one provides counsel and correction to perfect one's virtue.
These were the words of Tang and Gaozong addressed to Fu Yue, as seen in the "Shuo Ming" chapter of the *Shangshu*. "A" means to lean upon; "heng" means level.
"A-heng" was an official title of the Shang dynasty, signifying that which the world leans upon for leveling. It is also called "Bao-heng," or alternatively, it is said to be a title of Yi Yin.
In the *Taijia* chapter of the *Shangshu*,
it is recorded that Deng Tong,
a kinsman of Empress Dowager Jiao of Emperor Wen of the Han dynasty, was examined by a physiognomist who said, "He shall die of starvation. The Emperor replied, "Can he?"
As for the one named Tong who was wealthy, the Emperor subsequently granted him the copper mountains of the Shu region;

he cast coins that filled the world. Later, when misfortune befell him, he fled to a commoner’s house and eventually died of starvation. This is recorded in the *Jiangjian* (Outline of the Mirror) as well as the *Book of the Western Han*.

Regarding Jingu: this is the name of the garden belonging to Shi Chong. Shi Chong was a man of the Jin dynasty. He once vied with Wang Kai in a contest of wealth. Wang Kai [possessed] *shanzhu*... [text fragment ends].
There was a *hu* vessel about two chi tall, which [the Emperor] showed as a mark of honor. [The Prince] smashed it with an iron *ruyi*.
He then took six or seven stalks that were three or four chi tall and gave them to him. This is recorded in the Jin History (*Jin shi*) and various historical accounts (*gushi shu*).
Regarding "Wuku" (Armory) by Wang Bo: the "Preface to the Pavilion of the Prince of Teng" states, "The armory of General Wang," meaning that there is nothing it does not contain.
It is like white jade without a single flaw.
The poem says: "A flaw in white jade may still be polished away; but a flaw in these words cannot be remedied. The commentary states:
"It is because a flaw or breakage in jade may still be ground and polished until it is smooth, whereas once speech has been lost, there is no way to recover it.
How profound and earnest is this warning! Therefore, Nan Rong repeated this chapter three times each day, and for this reason, Confucius [entrusted his sister's son to him]."
The *Shijing* (Book of Poetry) records that [the Duke of Zhou] gave his daughter in marriage to him; this appears in the "Tang" chapter of the *Daya*.

The *Guangyun* states that "longzhong" refers to an elderly person in a decrepit state. It also notes that "longzhong" is the name of a bamboo species produced on Mount Luofu. The *Danyanlu* says: "When a person grows old, they resemble a bamboo swaying back and forth."
He did not hold onto it [as a mere possession].

He earnestly applied it to his breast, adhering to the Doctrine of the Mean. The Master said, "As for the character of Hui, he chooses from within the Mean; whenever he obtains one good thing, he then earnestly applies it to his breast."
"He embraces it and does not lose it. The commentary states: Hui was the name of Yan Yuan, a disciple of Confucius. *Quanquan* describes the manner of reverently upholding [the teachings].
*Fu* means "to wear" or "to manifest. *Ying* refers to the chest. It means to uphold [the teachings] and manifest them within the space of one's heart and mind;
this speaks of his ability to maintain them. Yanzi truly understood them; therefore, he was able to choose and maintain them in such a manner.

"Do not be presumptuous; do not be compulsive" (*Analects*). "The Master severed four things: do not be presumptuous, do not be compulsive, do not be obstinate, and do not be self-centered. The commentary states: "Severed" means to eliminate them completely.
"Mu" (毋) is written as "wu" (無) in the *Shiji*; it means "not to. "Yi" (意) refers to private intention. "Bi" (必) refers to insistence or expectation.

"Gu" (固) refers to stubborn attachment. "Wo" (我) refers to the self. These four function as a cycle of beginning and end: they originate in intention, proceed to insistence, linger in attachment, and culminate in the self.
Generally, intention and insistence always precede an event, while attachment and the self always follow after; yet from the self, the cycle arises once more.
If the mind is thus, one will be led astray by worldly desires in an endless cycle. Chengzi said: "This word 'wu' (do not) is not a term of prohibition.
Since the Sage has already severed these four things, what need would there be for prohibition?"
Since the skin no longer exists:
In the winter of the fourteenth year of Duke Xi of Lu, Qin suffered from famine and sent an envoy to beg for grain from Jin. The people of Jin would not grant it. Qing Zheng said:

"To turn one's back on favors is to lack intimacy; to rejoice at another's calamity is inhumane; to covet and receive [goods] is inauspicious; to provoke a neighbor is unrighteous. These four virtues are all..."
[The King] lost [the city]. How can one maintain a state? Guo She said: "If the hide no longer exists, where shall the fur be attached? The commentary states: Qing Zheng was a high official of Jin;

Guo She was the maternal uncle of Duke Hui. Previously, Duke Hui had promised to bribe the state of Qin with five cities in order to seek entry into his own country, but he subsequently reneged on this promise.
Therefore, Guo She used the "hide" as a metaphor for the cities and the "fur" as a metaphor for the grain, saying that since he would not grant them to Qin...
The city’s enmity has already become deep; though one now bestows grain upon it, it is like applying hair where there is no skin—there is nothing for it to adhere to.
Excerpted from the *Commentary on the Spring and Autumn Annals* (Chunqiu Zuozhuan Zhupingce), Volume Eleven.
*Fahua Dacheng Yinyi*, Scroll Four.
"He who believes without words is Heaven. The gentleman says:
"Ritual and music must not for a single moment be removed from one's person. To bring forth music to harmonize the mind results in ease, straightforwardness, and filiality."
A heart of sincerity arises spontaneously. When the heart of straightforwardness, uprightness, benevolence, and sincerity arises, there is joy. Joy leads to peace; peace leads to endurance;
endurance leads to heaven-likeness; heaven-likeness leads to spiritual power. Being like heaven, one is trusted without speaking; being spiritual, one is majestic without anger.
"To bring forth music is to cultivate the mind. The commentary states: "To 'bring forth' (zhì) means to investigate and exhaustively study its principles.
Since music issues from within, it is spoken of in terms of cultivating the mind. Ziliang: Following Zhu Xi’s interpretation, read [the character] as *cíliáng* (benevolent and good).

When music moves and transforms the human heart, it reaches the level of Heaven and the divine; through this, one can recognize the subtlety of exhausting the root and knowing change. From the *Liji*.
The "Jile" (Record of Joy) chapter of the *Mengzi*:
"To possess within oneself is called faith (*xin*).
Hao Sheng Bu Hai asked, "What kind of person was Yue Zhengzi? Mencius replied, "He was a man of goodness; he was a man of faith."
"What is meant by 'good' (shàn)? What is meant by 'trustworthiness' (xìn)? He replied: "That which is desirable is called good; that which one possesses within oneself is called trustworthiness.
The commentary states: "All that is called good must actually exist [within oneself]. It further says: "To be truly good in one's person is called trustworthiness.
This is from the "Jinxin" chapter of the *Mencius*.

"If one has not yet gained their trust, they will consider it an oppression," says the *Analects*. Zi Xia said: "A gentleman, having first gained the trust of his people, then exerts them in labor; if he has not yet gained their trust, they will consider it an oppression against themselves.
Having first gained their trust, he then offers remonstrance; if he has not yet gained their trust, they will consider it slander against themselves."
The *Qingnang* was seen by the simple woman Hua Tuo, whose courtesy name was Yuanhua. He was a native of Qiao Commandery in Pei Commandery. His skillful hands were rarely matched in the world.
After Cao Cao was struck by the "Pear Tree Spirit Sword" in a dream, his headache would not cease. He summoned Hua Tuo, who—
Regarding the words "Hemp-Lung Decoction" and "Shattering the Brain," Cao suspected him of treachery and had him seized and cast into prison.
The jailer in the prison was surnamed Wu; he was known as "Wu the Jail Overseer. This man daily provided Hua Tuo with wine and food.

Grateful for this kindness, Hua Tuo told him: "I am now to die an untimely death. I possess a book titled *Qing Nang* (The Green Bag) which has not yet been transmitted to the world. I am deeply grateful [for your service]."
"Your kindness cannot be repaid. I shall compose a letter; send one person to my house to retrieve a book from a blue bag and deliver it to you, so that you may continue my divine efficacy.
The prison warden of Wu said, "If I obtain this book, I shall abandon this post and practice medicine throughout the world to fully realize the Master's virtue. Da then composed the letter.
He said to the jailer Wu, "When I was about to arrive, I gave this letter to my wife and had her hide it.
After taking his leave of Hua Tuo, the jailer Wu went directly to Jin City and asked for the letter from Hua Tuo’s wife, who had it hidden away as instructed.
After the jailer Wu returned home, he ordered his wife to conceal it. Ten days later, Cao Cao’s illness grew increasingly severe, and Hua Tuo died in prison. The jailer Wu...
Having finished his corvée labor, he returned home and asked his wife for the medical manual. He sought a physician to treat his illness, but his wife said, "I have already burned it.
When her husband asked why, she replied, "Even if you were to master this medicine as well as Hua Tuo himself, you would still end up dying in prison.
That is why I destroyed it. Consequently, the *Qingnang* manual was not transmitted to the world. A later scholar wrote a poem on this: [Poem omitted per instructions.]
The divine physician’s marvelous hand was most excellent; he inherited the "Sea-side Prescriptions" of the Immortal. That a foolish woman burned them is truly lamentable;
henceforth, later generations could no longer behold the "Green Sack. (This is detailed in the *Records of the Three Kingdoms*. The rhinoceros banner fell into the hands of a favorite concubine.
The *xīdào* is the standard of the great general. If it falls into the hands of a favorite concubine, there will surely be unforeseen calamity;
if it truly belongs to such a person, then its origins cannot be verified.

When requesting instruction, one rises and sits as an attendant before the teacher (*xiansheng*). When the teacher questions him, he responds only after the questioning has concluded. When requesting a new subject of study, he rises;

when requesting further explanation of what he already knows, he rises. The commentary states: "To 'request further explanation' means to ask again about the remaining depths of the matter that have not yet been fully understood. One rises in order to show reverence. (From the *Liji*)
From the "Qu Li" (Ceremonial Etiquette) chapter:

When a new topic is introduced, one rises while attending as a seated guest before a gentleman (*junzi*). When the gentleman asks about a new topic, the guest rises and responds. Lüshi said: "Asking about a new topic..."

As for those who rise to respond [to a superior], they do so because their conduct undergoes change due to specific circumstances, thereby giving rise to reverence. This is from the "Qu Li" (Ceremonial Etiquette) chapter of the *Liji* (Book of Rites).

When Zheng was besieged by Duke Zhuang of Chu, he captured it. Duke Xiang of Zheng bared his upper body, led a sheep forward, and went out to meet him, saying: "I, your humble servant, have been unfortunate."
"I was unable to serve my sovereign, causing him to harbor resentment against our humble state; this is the fault of my solitary self.
How could I dare not simply obey whatever command you give? (etc. Quoted from the *Zuo Zhuan*.
"One does not know the true face of Mount Lu.
When Dongpo visited Mount Lu and arrived at Donglin, he composed two verses, saying: "The sound of the stream is entirely the broad and long tongue;
The color of the mountains is nothing but the pure and serene body. Last night there were eighty-four thousand verses; How shall I present them to others on another day?"
Viewed from the side, they are ridges; viewed from the front, they are peaks. Seen from afar or nearby, the mountains appear entirely different.
One does not recognize the true face of Mount Lu, simply because one is standing within the mountain itself. Master Shan谷 said: "This old man speaks of *prajñā* both horizontally and vertically."
There are no superfluous words here. Were it not for those with a voice from the tip of their pen, how could such an untransmitted marvel be uttered?
One may see this in the *Youxi Sanmei* (Samādhi of Play), the *Chanxi Ji* (Anthology of Zen Joy), and the *Zhengwen Lu* (Record of Inquiries).

When they were departing from the room of Vimalakīrti to pay homage at the seats, there was a celestial maiden who took heavenly flowers and scattered them over the bodhisattvas and the great disciples (*mahāśrāvaka*).
When the flowers reached the bodhisattvas, they all fell away; but when they reached the great disciples, they stuck to them and did not fall. All the disciples...
The son used his supernatural power to remove the flowers, but he was unable to make them go away. The goddess asked Śāriputra, "For what reason do you remove these flowers?
He replied, "These flowers are not in accordance with the Dharma; therefore, I remove them. The goddess said, "Do not say that these flowers are not in accordance with the Dharma.

These flowers have no discriminating thoughts; it is you, Venerable One, who give rise to the notion of discrimination. Because your habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) are not yet exhausted, the flowers cling to your body."
[It is] as follows: for one whose habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) are exhausted, the flowers do not adhere. The details of this appear in the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra*.
Vimalakīrti said to Śāriputra, "Take a seat upon the lion-throne. Śāriputra said, "This throne is high and broad; I cannot ascend it.
The gentleman [Vimalakīrti] said, "Śāriputra, simply pay homage to the Tathāgata Sumerudīparāja, and then you will be able to sit. Thereupon, Śāriputra...
Having paid homage, he immediately obtained this seat. The details are found in the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*.
At that time, when Sudhana reached the city of Tāladhvaja, he saw King Aśoka (the Unwearied) holding countless criminals and inflicting upon them the punishments of a king.
Suffering intense agony, Sudhana thought to himself, "For the benefit of all sentient beings, I seek the conduct of a bodhisattva and cultivate the path of a bodhisattva.
