Yet this king is in such a state; how can he seek the Dharma? At that moment, he heard a voice from the sky, and immediately went to where the king was.

He prostrated at his feet and said, "Noble One, I have already set my mind upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, yet I do not know how to learn the conduct of a bodhisattva or cultivate the path of a bodhisattva.
At that time, the King said to Sudhana, "If I had truly committed such evil deeds, how could I have obtained such a karmic fruit?
It was for the sake of taming sentient beings and causing them to develop [the resolve for awakening]..."
The Bodhicitta. From the sixty-sixth fascicle of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*:
"When Śikhin showed him the fire-roasting, at that time Sudhana went to the village of Īśāna and saw that Śikhin was practicing various ascetic penances, seeking..."
Omniscience. On all four sides were masses of fire like great mountains, within which stood a mountain of swords, towering and infinitely steep.
Ascending that mountain, he cast himself into the flames. At that time, Sudhana prostrated at his feet and said:
"Noble One, I have already set my mind upon Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, yet I do not know how to learn the conduct of a bodhisattva or cultivate the path of a bodhisattva. The Brahmin—
He said, "If you can ascend this mountain of blades and cast yourself into this mass of fire, all the practices of the bodhisattvas will become completely purified.
Sudhana thought to himself, "It is difficult to obtain a human body; it is difficult to be free from all obstacles and hindrances...

At that time, the eight classes of spirits and deities said to Sudhana, "This brahmin has been performing the 'five heats' asceticism and preaching the Dharma for us, causing us to feel love and joy without end."
He attained supreme enlightenment. Upon hearing this, Sudhana rejoiced and repented his past transgressions; he then immediately climbed the mountain and cast himself into the fire.
Before he had even reached the midpoint, he attained the Samādhi of the Well-Abiding Bodhi. This is the source from which the sixty-four fascicles of the Avataṃsaka Sūtra emerged.
Regarding the "Cold Wind" (Hanfeng): during the eight nights before and after the winter solstice, the cold wind split the bamboo; the Buddha requested two robes to ward off the cold.
This is seen in the ninth fascicle of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*.
The *Bimbasāra-sūtra* states: In the kingdom of Rājagṛha, there was a Brahmin king named Ajātaśatru, who was intelligent and possessed great wisdom.
He asked Sudatta, "Are there any divine beings in this land worthy of veneration? Sudatta replied, "There are."
Prince Da (Druma) left the household life and attained Buddhahood, becoming one honored by devas and humans.

Ajita went to the Buddha’s dwelling and addressed the Buddha, saying, "I pray that the Buddha and the Sangha will accept my invitation for the three-month summer retreat. The Buddha said, "I have many followers here. The King said:

He did not consider this to be much. Thus it was repeated three times. The Buddha and five hundred bhikṣus accepted the invitation and went to the kingdom, staying beneath the trees in a forest to the north of the city.
The Buddha instructed the bhikṣus: "This town is impoverished and cramped; many people lack faith, and alms are difficult to obtain.
Those who wish to observe the rains retreat may stay; others may go as they please. At that time, Śāriputra accepted the invitation from Śakra and the asuras.
The women entreated him. At that time, a celestial Māra deluded the king’s mind, and he returned to the inner palace and commanded the gatekeepers:
"For three months, no matter how great or small the matter, none shall be announced. Thus, the bhikṣu found it difficult to beg for alms. Maudgalyāyana informed the Buddha.

"There is a tree named Jambu; I wish to take its fruit to provide for the assembly. In Uttarakuru there is naturally grown non-glutinous rice, and in the Trāyastriṃśa heaven there is the food of the gods and the flavors of the asuras;
I wish to take these all to provide for the great multitude. We pray that the Buddha will grant us permission. The Buddha did not grant permission.
There was a horse-herder who said to the bhikṣus, "I have barley for horses; would you be able to eat it? The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha accordingly accepted it.
There were five hundred horses; each horse consumed two *śēng* daily, and they divided half of this with the Saṃgha.
There was one excellent horse that consumed four *śēng* daily; they divided half of this to offer to the Buddha. Ānanda took the Buddha’s portion as well as his own, and carried them inside.
In a certain village, he saw a woman and said to Ānanda, "I shall prepare a meal for you. When it was cooked, Ānanda took the food and offered it to the Buddha, who then accepted it.
At that time, when the people of the country heard that the Buddha had been eating horse fodder, they prepared various offerings for him.

Seven days remained until the end of the *pravāraṇā*. The Buddha told Ānanda, "Enter the city and inform the King that the rains retreat has concluded and that we shall travel again through other kingdoms.
Ānanda went to the King’s presence and delivered the Buddha’s words. The King asked where the Buddha was.
Ānanda replied, "He accepted the King’s invitation for three months; he is still in the kingdom for that reason. The King asked who provided his sustenance. Ānanda replied, "Only..."
[The Buddha] ate horse fodder. The King then first attained awakening and went to the Buddha to repent. The *Xingqi xing jing* (Sūtra on the Arising of Practice) says:
The Buddha told Śāriputra, "In the past, there was a Buddha named Vipaśyin. There was a king named Bandhumat and a brahmin named Indragiri who taught five hundred youths.
At that time, the king prepared a vegetarian feast and invited the Buddha. There was a bhikṣu named..."
“Maitreya, I was ill and unable to walk. After I had finished my meal, I requested food for the sick man, but the brahmin would not give it to him.
He reviled me, saying: ‘Shaven-headed śramaṇa, you ought to eat horse fodder; you should not eat such sweet and delicious offerings.
At that time, the young boys said, ‘It is truly so. Śāriputra, the brahmin at that time was none other than myself. The five hundred boys are now...”

The five hundred bhikṣus were these very ones; the sick bhikṣu was Maitreya, who is now [the Bodhisattva]. Furthermore, see the fifth fascicle of the *Jinglü yìxiàng* (Heterogeneous Phenomena of Sūtra and Vinaya):
"The River Lord and the Well-Frog."

When the autumn waters arrive in their season, the hundred rivers pour into the River. The current of the Jing is so vast that between its two banks and its islands and shores, one cannot distinguish oxen from horses.
Thereupon, the Lord of the River is filled with joy and self-satisfaction, deeming all the beauty in the world to be contained entirely within himself.
Flowing eastward with the current, he reached the Northern Sea. Facing east and looking out, he could not see the end of the water.
Thereupon, Lord of the River first turned his face around; gazing across the vast expanse toward Ruo, he sighed and said, "There is a common saying: 'To have heard but a hundred ways of the Dao...'"
"To think that no one could equal me—that is what I used to say. Furthermore, I have heard of those who disparaged the learning of Zhongni and slighted the righteousness of Boyi;
at first I did not believe it. Now that I have encountered the inexhaustible depth of your [teachings], I realize that had I not come to your gate, I would have been in peril.
I would have been held in perpetual derision by the masters of the Great Way."—The North Sea [God].
If it is said that a frog in a well cannot be spoken to about the ocean because it is confined to its pit; that a summer insect cannot be spoken to about ice because it is bound by its season;

and that a pedantic scholar cannot be spoken to about the Way because he is fettered by his teachings—now you have emerged from the shore and gazed upon the great sea, whereupon you shall know your own insignificance. You may now be spoken to.
It is truly great! Among all the waters under heaven, none are greater than the sea. Myriad streams flow into it, yet one knows not when they cease, for it does not overflow;
the Tailgate (Weilu) drains from it, yet one knows not when it ends, for it is never emptied. It remains unchanged through spring and autumn, and takes no notice of flood or drought.
Its superiority over the currents of the Yangtze and the Yellow River cannot be measured by numbers, yet I have never [regarded it as such].
"As for this 'self' being so much: it compares its own form to heaven and earth and receives its vital breath from yin and yang.
My existence within heaven and earth is like a small pebble or a tiny sapling upon Mount Tai. This is excerpted from the "Autumn Floods" chapter of the *Zhuangzi*.
"Acting without acting"—Mencius said:
"That which acts without being acted upon is Heaven; that which arrives without being brought about is Destiny. [In such a state,] the currency strings rot and the grain becomes moldy.
At the beginning of Emperor Wu of the Han dynasty, the coins in the capital accumulated to tens of millions; the strings were so worn out that they could not even be counted.
In the Grand Granary, the grain lay piled one upon another in successive layers, overflowing until it was stored in open piles outside, rotting red and unfit for consumption. (See *Shiji*.)
Táo Hóng (蕭宏), younger brother of Emperor Wu of the Liang dynasty, was enfeoffed as the Prince of Linchuan. He was fond of money;

he would gather millions in one place and mark them with a yellow banner, or store tens of millions in a single treasury and hang a purple banner over it. There were more than ten such rooms. When Emperor Wu saw this, he calculated the total amount of money.

There were more than three hundred million [coins]. His storehouses were filled with other goods, regardless of their quantity. Xiao Zong composed the "Discourse on the Folly of Coinage" (*Qian yu lun*) to satirize him;
this is recorded in the *Liang shi* (History of the Liang), which is a collection of historical records.

"Regarding 'embodying the middle way for the various ministers,' the Master said: 'In governing the world and the state, there are nine constant courses. They are: cultivating one's own person; honoring the worthy; being affectionate toward kinsmen;
respecting great ministers; embodying the middle way for the various ministers; treating the common people as one's children; welcoming the various artisans; and being gentle with the military.'"

"He keeps people at a distance" means he cherishes the feudal lords. The commentary states: "Jing" (經) means "constant. "Ti" (體) refers to imagining oneself in their position and observing their minds.
"Revering one's nature and inquiring through learning constitute the Mean.

Therefore, the gentleman reveres his nature and takes the path of inquiry and learning. The commentary states: "Revering one's nature is the means by which he preserves the mind and reaches the ultimate greatness of the Way’s essence.
Taking the path of inquiry and learning is the means by which he brings knowledge to completion and exhausts the Way."
The subtlety of its essence. These two are the primary principles for cultivating virtue and consolidating the Way.

Regarding "those nearby are pleased and those afar come," from the *Analects*: When the Duke of She asked about government, the Master said, "Those nearby are pleased; those afar come. The commentary states: "When they are covered by its bounty..."
Joyful, they come upon hearing its reputation; yet it is always those nearby who are first pleased, and only then do those from afar arrive.

At that time, when two hundred questions had arisen, the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra, knowing that the assembly had gathered, addressed the Bodhisattva Samantamukha, saying: "O Son of the Buddha, please [speak] for us."
"Please expound upon this: what is the reliance of a bodhisattva mahāsattva? What is the extraordinary perception?
And for what reason does the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, manifest parinirvāṇa? Excellent, O Son of the Buddha! We pray that you will expound such dharmas as these.
At that time, Samantabhadra Bodhisattva addressed the Bodhisattvas, including Samantamati and the others, saying: "O Sons of the Buddha, regarding the bodhi..."
O Mahāsattva, there are ten kinds of bases and ten kinds of extraordinary conceptions.
Furthermore, when the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha has completed his buddha-work, he manifests parinirvāṇa by contemplating ten kinds of meanings;

the details of this appear in the "Detachment from the World" chapter (*Lokottara-parivarta*) of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*. Regarding the phrase "cloud-rising and pitcher-pouring," it refers to two bodhisattvas who act as questioners, their inquiries arising like clouds.
Chang-k'ung replied: "It is like pouring water from an overturned jar; thus the *Fǎhuá* praises it, saying, 'The Universal Worthy pours from his jar to repay in two thousand ways.
(From *Fǎhuá Dàchéng Yīnyì*, Volume Five)

"Clouds and dragons, wind and tigers"—this is from the *Book of Changes*. The Master said: "Those of the same sound respond to one another; those of the same breath seek one another out. Water flows toward moisture; fire moves toward dryness.

Clouds follow dragons; wind follows tigers. When the Sage arises, all things behold him. That which is rooted in Heaven is kin to what is above; that which is rooted in Earth [is kin to what is below]."
Those who are close follow downward; thus each follows its own kind. The Imperial Decree proclaims:

"The words of a king are like a single strand of silk; once they issue forth, they are like a twisted cord. The words of a king are like a twisted cord; once they issue forth, they are like a thick rope. The commentary states: [This refers to how the influence of the sovereign expands from subtle beginnings to great magnitude.]
"Lun-shou" refers to the silk cords; "fei" refers to the large ropes used to pull the coffin.
This is from the "Zi Yi" chapter of the *Liji*.

At that time, the World-Honored One, the predecessor of Feili, gave rise to wisdom and insight, knowing that Udāraka Rāmaputra was currently in the Sphere of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*).
Having ended their lives there, they later fall back down and are born in this place, taking the body of a flying weasel.
Whatever sentient beings are born in the water, or dwell on land, or fly through the air, they shall kill them at every turn; when their retribution is exhausted, they die of starvation.
The World-Honored One, having attained enlightenment, desired to go and deliver him [Rāmaputra]. Seven days had already passed since his death, yet there was a verse that said:

"The World-Honored One, wishing to speak of Rāmaputra, resolved to observe where he had been reborn; knowing that he had now died and was in the heavens, he thought in his mind of the five *ṛṣis* and desired to go to them.
(From the *Buddhacarita-saṃyukta-sūtra*, Scroll 33; cited in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, Vol. 10).

The ninth fascicle states: Udraka Rāmaputra attained the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception and possessed the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*). Day after day he would fly into the royal palace to eat.

The king’s consort, according to the laws of her country, prostrated herself by touching his feet in greeting; upon this contact with his feet, his desire was aroused and he lost his supernormal powers.

He requested a carriage to return to the mountains, where he again cultivated the five supernormal powers. With single-minded devotion, he was on the verge of attaining meditative absorption when [he encountered] the forest in which he relied...
In a pond, amidst the clamor of various fish and birds, he made a malicious vow to devour them all.

Later, when his concentration returned to its former state, he was reborn in the Sphere of Neither-Perception-nor-Non-perception (Naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana). When his retribution there was exhausted, he was drawn by his prior vow and fell into the body of a flying fox.

As stated in the *Buddhanāmasūtra*, the Buddha said to Śāriputra: "Your teacher Udraka Rāmaputra attained the meditative absorption of neither-perception-nor-non-perception for eighty thousand [kalpas]."
When the four thousand kalpas were completed, after his life came to an end, he could not avoid being reborn again as a flying weasel.
This was because while practicing this meditative concentration, he had been disturbed by the clamor of crows in the forest and the noise of fish and other creatures near the water;

his mind gave rise to anger, and he vowed, "May I enter the water and fly through the air to devour them. Once the power of his concentration was exhausted, he immediately received this retribution. (See the *Jǐngjué jīng lüècāo*).
Fascicle Eleven. The Buddha spoke of the future existence of the monk Kṣema-darśin:
"In the city of Śrāvastī, there was an old mother of the householder Sudatta who did not wish to see the Buddha. While the Buddha was [staying]..."

She stood before him shielding herself with a fan. The Buddha caused her fan to become like a mirror, so that there was no obstruction; in the four directions, above, and below, there was only the Buddha.
She covered her face with her hands, and all ten fingers transformed into Buddhas. The old woman did not believe, so the Buddha commanded Rāhula to convert her.
Rāhula transformed himself into a Wheel-Turning King and went to the elder’s house to proclaim the sublime Dharma. The old...
Having heard this, the mother’s heart was filled with joy, and she went to the Buddha’s dwelling to renounce the householder’s life.

King Prasenajit and Queen Mallikā paid homage to the Buddha and said: “What transgression did this old woman commit in her past lives that she was born into such a lowly station as a servant to others?
And what merit and blessings has she accumulated that she now encounters the World-Honored One? The Buddha said: “In the past, there was a Buddha named Ratnacchatradīparāja.”
After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, during the period of the Semblance Dharma, there was a king named Citraratnapuṣpaprabha. He had a son named Sudarśana who wished to leave the household life.
The king granted him permission, and he subsequently went into the mountains where he became a disciple of a certain bhikṣu.
"He slandered his teacher, saying he was empty and lacked wisdom; may I never again see him in future lives. My *ācārya* possessed wisdom and eloquence;
may he be my spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) in birth after birth. Because of his erroneous understanding, after his life ended, he fell into the Avīci Hell.
At that time, the *upādhyāya* was none other than my current self; the *ācārya* was none other than Rāhula, the Prince.
"Monk, this old woman here is she. (From the *Buddhasamādhi-sāgara-sūtra*, fascicle six).
Regarding the "six teachers' followers":
as for the "six teachers," one is named Pūraṇa; Kāśyapa is his clan name. Second is Makkhali... [text continues].
1. Pūraṇa is his name; Kūṭadanta is the son’s name derived from his mother’s. 2. Maskarin is his name;
Śariputra is the son’s name derived from his mother’s. 3. Ajita is his name; Keśakambala is the name of his coarse garment.
4. Kakuda is his name; Kātyāyana is his clan name. 5. Nirgrantha is his name; Jñātiputra is the son’s name derived from his mother’s. Thus they are seen.
In the *Huayan Xuantan* (Suspended Discourse on the Avatamsaka), it says: "A mantis cannot block the tracks [of a chariot].
Qu Boyu answered Yan He, saying: 'Do you not know that mantis? It bristles its back in anger to confront a chariot.'"
Zhe. He did not realize he was incapable of the task. (From the "Renjian Shi" chapter of the *Zhuangzi*). Shi. Duke Zhuang of Qi went out hunting.
There was a mantis that raised its legs, intending to strike his chariot wheel. He asked his charioteer, "What kind of insect is this? The charioteer replied: [The text continues from here].
It was a mantis. This insect knows how to advance but not how to retreat; it does not measure its own strength but recklessly challenges the enemy.
The Duke said, "This is the bravest of insects in the world. He turned his chariot to avoid it, and thus the brave warrior returned home.
"Thirty spokes converge upon a single hub.
The *Dàodé jīng* says: "Thirty spokes converge upon a single hub; it is through its emptiness that the utility of the chariot exists. The *Jīngjiě* (Precise Explanation) says:
The spokes are the limbs of the wheel. The hub is that which contains the axle within the wheel; it is the heart of the wheel. "Dang" means "only.
To be empty in the center is called "non-being. Only when the hub is empty in its center can the axle be turned and the vehicle move. Therefore it is said: "There is the utility of the vehicle."
The people could not bear to cut down the sweet pear tree;

the *Shi* says: "Lush and verdant is the sweet pear tree; do not trim it, do not cut it down; it was where the Earl of Shao took shelter. The commentary states: This is a *fu* (narrative) verse. "Bìfèi" means lush and verdant.
"Flourishing appearance. *Gantang* (Sweet Pear Tree) refers to the *duli* (Chinese pear). Those that are white are called *tang*, while those that are red are called *du*.

"Shearing" (*jian*) means to trim its branches and leaves; "felling" (*fa*) means to cut down its twigs and trunk. "Duke" (*bo*) refers to the Regional Duke (*fangbo*). "Thatch hut" (*bai*) is a dwelling made of grass.

When the Duke of Shao conducted tours through the southern states to disseminate the governance of King Wen, he sometimes took shelter beneath a sweet pear tree. Later generations, remembering his virtue, [preserved it]. Thus...
He loved the trees and could not bear to harm them. "Zhao" is the name of a place; it was the fief of the Duke of Shao, Shao Gong Xi.

Traditional accounts state that south of Yong County in Fufeng lay Zhao Ting (the Pavilion of Zhao), which was precisely this location. Today, Yong County has been divided into Qishan and Tianxing counties, so it is unknown in which county Zhao Ting specifically lies.
This is recorded in the "Shao Nan" (South of Zhao) chapter of the *Guofeng* (Airs of the States) and in the various biographies of the states.
"The Way exists in a single glance;
when Zhongni saw Wen Bo Xuezi, he did not speak. Zi Lu asked, "Master, you have long desired to see Wen Bo Xuezi;
why is it that upon seeing him, you do not speak? Zhongni replied, "As for such a person, one perceives him through a mere glance."
"The Way exists; it cannot even accommodate a sound. (From the "Outer Chapters" of the *Zhuangzi*).
"It is not that sprouts do not grow there.
Mencius said: "The trees on Mount Niu were once beautiful. Because it borders a great state, axes and hatchets have felled them."
Can it be considered beautiful? It is because of the rest it receives day and night, and the nourishment provided by rain and dew, that sprouts and shoots do not fail to grow there.
*The Analects*, "Looking at it, it is ahead": Yan Yuan sighed deeply and said, "Looking up at it, it is ever more high; drilling into it, it is ever more solid. Looking at it, it is ahead;

suddenly, it is behind. The commentary states: *Quèi* is the sound of a sigh. "Looking up, it is ever more high" means it is unattainable. "Drilling into it, it is ever more solid" means it cannot be penetrated.
Entering, he was sometimes before and sometimes behind; he was so ethereal and indistinct that he could not be represented by any fixed image.
This was Yanzi’s profound realization that the Way of the Master is inexhaustible and devoid of spatial or corporeal limits, and his expression of wonder at it.

"Eye, knowledge, clarity, and awakening; eye, knowledge, and so forth" refers to the stage of the path of vision (*darśanamārga*). Here, the patience regarding the dharma of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-kṣānti*) is the eye; the knowledge regarding the dharma of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna*) is knowledge;

the subsequent patience regarding suffering (*duḥkha-anvaya-kṣānti*) is clarity; and the subsequent knowledge regarding suffering (*duḥkha-anvaya-jñāna*) is awakening. This is extracted from the fifth fascicle of the *Fuxing* (Subcommentary). The Tripiṭaka Master Paramārtha stated:

The "eye of wisdom" (prajñā-cakṣus) serves as the general category, while "knowledge" (jñāna), "clarity" (vidyā), and "awakening" (bodhi) serve as the specific distinctions. Knowledge comprehends the past; clarity penetrates the future; and awakening discerns the present.
This concludes the record on the divergent tenets of various schools.

Regarding rites, music, and military expeditions, the *Analects* records that Confucius said: "When the Way prevails in the world, rites, music, and military expeditions issue forth from the Son of Heaven.
When the Way does not prevail in the world, rites, music, and military expeditions issue forth from the feudal lords."

Regarding the passage from the *Daodejing*: "The superior person, upon hearing the Way, practices it with diligence; the mediocre person, upon hearing the Way, is as if it exists and as if it does not;
the inferior person, upon hearing the Way, laughs at it. If they did not laugh, it would not be fit to be called the Way. The *Jingjie* (Precise Explanation) states: "Upon hearing it, one must..."
Faith, therefore, is the fruit of practice. To both believe and doubt—whether thinking something exists or thinking it does not—is the way of the most base and vulgar, who simply laugh at it.
Only when the lowest of people take it as a cause for laughter do we truly perceive the loftiness of our Way.
*Fahua Dacheng Yinyi*, Scroll Six: "Qian Qian" (Ever Vigilant and Unceasing), *Zhouyi*, Hexagram Qian.
"The superior man is ever vigilant and unceasing all day long. The Image says: "The movement of Heaven is vigorous; the superior man, accordingly, exerts himself with strength."
"Unceasing. The commentary states: "Qianqian (strenuous and alert) is the image of being apprehensive and cautious.

Regarding judging a person by their outward appearance, Confucius said: 'If one judges a person by their countenance, one will fail with Zi Yu; if one judges a person by their words, one will fail with Zai Wo.'"
As for my statement that Confucius said [the person] "lost it," this was intended only to make people understand that one cannot judge a person based on their words and appearance;
thus, while the wording is the same as in the *Shiji*, the underlying meaning is actually the opposite. This is seen in the *Kongzi Jiayu*.
At that time, when Śāriputra and Rādha were competing for preeminence, the elder Sudatta had fathered seven sons. Each had taken a wife, but the seventh son remained unmarried;
he was subsequently wedded to the daughter of the elder Ghoṣila of the city. Upon seeing the extensive array of offerings prepared by Ghoṣila’s household, [he was moved].
He immediately asked, "What is it that you intend to do? He replied, "I have invited the Buddha and the Sangha. Sudatta asked, "Who is called the Buddha? Pūrṇa replied, "Have you not heard?
The son of King Śuddhodana has left the household life and attained Buddhahood. If you go to see him, you will obtain immeasurable merit.
Sudatta was filled with joy and went to the place where the World-Honored One was. The World-Honored One bade him sit. At that time, Śūdra...

At that time, the gods transformed themselves into four men who approached in a procession. They circumambulated him three times to the right, knelt with their right knees touching the ground, and withdrew to stand to one side.
Sudatta paid his respects in that manner, and the World-Honored One immediately preached the Dharma for him, enabling him to attain the first fruit of the path.

Sudatta then asked the World-Honored One, "In the city of Śrāvastī, many people believe in heterodox teachings; why does the Buddha not deliver them? The Buddha replied, "They have no [receptive] basis."

"How shall we proceed with the construction? Sudatta addressed the Buddha, saying, "I, your disciple, am able to undertake this; I pray that you will grant me your permission. The World-Honored One remained silent.
Sudatta, together with Śāriputra, searched everywhere until they found that only Prince Jeta’s garden was suitable for building a vihāra.
He then addressed the Prince, offering to cover the ground with gold. This moved the Prince, and together they established the vihāra. Thus it was Sudatta who [completed] it.
[The king] was delighted. When the six teachers heard this, they went to inform the king: "Sudatta has purchased a garden, intending to establish a monastery for the śramaṇas.
Allow my disciples to compete with the multitude in a contest of skills. If the śramaṇa is victorious, then let him be permitted to build;
if he is not as capable, he shall not be allowed to do so. The king summoned Sudatta and asked him: "Now these six teachers wish to [compete] with the śramaṇa..."
"Let us compare our skills; if I am superior, I shall establish [the site], but if I am not superior, I may not. When Sudatta heard this, he became distressed and unhappy.
At that time, Śāriputra went to the elder’s house and asked, "For what reason are you unhappy? He replied:
Regarding the vihāra he had established, he feared it might not be completed, and for this reason he was displeased.

He then informed [Śāriputra] of the words of the six teachers. Śāriputra said, "Do as you wish; let us compare them. At that time, each prepared his own seat, and the drum was struck to assemble the multitude.
Then Śāriputra entered meditative concentration beneath a tree. Sudatta addressed him, saying, "Venerable One, the great assembly has gathered; I pray that you will come to the gathering. Śāriputra—
Without rising from his meditative concentration, he went to where the great assembly was gathered. When the assembly saw him, they rose spontaneously and paid their respects.
Śāriputra then ascended the seat. Among the six heretical teachers was a disciple named Raudrākṣa, who was skilled in the arts of illusion.
Before the great assembly, he used incantations to conjure a tree. Śāriputra, by means of his supernormal powers, manifested a whirlwind that blew it down to the ground.
Furthermore, he transformed himself by means of incantations into a pond whose four sides were composed of jewels. Within the pond grew various kinds of flowers.
Śāriputra then manifested as a white elephant with six tusks; upon each tusk were seven kinds of flowers, and upon each flower were seven jade maidens.
As the elephant approached the edge of the pond, the water immediately vanished. He then further manifested a mountain adorned with the seven treasures. Śāriputra...
Śāriputra transformed himself into a Vajrapāṇi and destroyed it with his mace;

he then transformed into a dragon, to which Śāriputra transformed into a golden-winged garuḍa king, who tore it apart and devoured it. He then transformed into an ox, to which Śāriputra transformed into a lion.
He split it and ate it. He then transformed back into the form of a yakṣa. Śāriputra manifested as the Heavenly King Vaiśravaṇa, and the yakṣa fled in terror.
A mass of fire surrounded him on all four sides, leaving him no place to go; only the space around Śāriputra remained cool and refreshing.
Rādha immediately bowed down in submission and sought mercy. Śāriputra ascended into the void and manifested the eighteen transformations before the assembled multitude.
The great assembly was filled with joy. Śāriputra then preached the Dharma for them. At that time, the disciples of the six heretical teachers left their homes to study the Way under Śāriputra.
The details of this account are found in the ninth fascicle of the *Sūtra on the Causes and Conditions of the Wise and the Foolish*.

Stuttering and halting like the Han Gaozu, Zhou Chang was ordered to deliver an imperial decree—intended to depose the heir apparent, the son of Empress Lü, and establish Liu Yirui, the son of Lady Qi—as known to all under heaven.
Unable to prevail in his opposition, Zhou Chang became enraged; therefore:
He replied, "Your servant is stammering and cannot obey Your Majesty's decree. "Qi-qi" refers to being slow of speech; thus he spoke with repetition, much like the modern expression "tied tongue.
Yang Xiong of the Han dynasty was slow of speech, and therefore his words were often repetitive. Deng Ai of the Wei dynasty was likewise slow of speech.
He was always called "Ai-ai" (Ei-ei), though those who saw him were not of one mind.

Regarding the way of managing affairs, the *I Ching* states: "Managing the affairs of one's father; having such a son ensures no blame for his father. Though perilous, there will ultimately be good fortune. The commentary says: "Managing the affairs of one's father."
"Yi (the intention) refers to the father. The commentary states: "Gan (the trunk) is like the trunk of a tree, that upon which the branches and leaves depend for their establishment.
Gu (decay/chaos) refers to the legacy left behind by previous generations that has been ruined. Therefore, all the hexagram lines contain the image of parents.
If the son can take up the 'gan' (trunk), he will then restore and revitalize it."
"A serene radiance appears upon his face.
Mencius said: "That which constitutes the nature of the superior man—benevolence, righteousness, ritual propriety, and wisdom—is rooted in the heart.

Its living color manifests as a serene radiance upon the face, overflowing from the back and extending through the four limbs; these four limbs speak without words. The commentary states: "Serenely radiant (sùrán)."
"Pure, harmonious, and lustrous appearance. "Aṅ" (盎) conveys the sense of being abundant, full, and overflowing. "Applied to the four limbs" means it is manifested in one's movements and deportment.

"Yù" (喻) means to inform or clarify. "The four limbs understand without words" means that the four limbs can naturally comprehend one’s intent without waiting for one’s spoken words. This is from the *Jinxin* chapter of the *Mencius*.

[The teachings of] the Duke of Wu and the Duke of Wen are spread throughout the tablets and slips of the *Zhongyong*. When Duke Ai asked about government, the Master said: "The governance of the Dukes Wen and Wu is spread throughout the tablets and slips.

When the person [who embodies it] exists, then that governance is implemented; when the person is gone, then that governance ceases. The commentary states: "Tablets" (*fang*) refers to wooden boards; "slips" (*ce*) refers to bamboo strips; "cease" (*xi*) means to perish.
Thus it is said: "Where there is such a ruler and such a minister, there is such a government.
As the *Daodejing* says regarding the Primordial Lord (*Xiangdi*): "He harmonizes his light and blends with the dust; he is profound and still, as if he were present. I do not know whose [he is]."
"Son! He is before the Primordial Lord (Xiangdi). The *Jingjie* (Essential Explanation) says: "To radiate light without being ostentatious is called 'harmonizing with the light';
to be free from dust yet not to be self-purifying is called 'being one with the dust. This is what the Buddhist scriptures mean by 'neither defiled nor pure.
If this is so, then that which is called the 'Ultimate Source' (Zong) is profound and eternally quiescent; it seems non-existent yet appears to exist. But who, indeed, is the son of such a being?"
I fear that even the Lord of Heaven would find this Way difficult to match. It seems it may have existed even before the Emperor.
According to the *Shifa* (Canon of Epithets), one whose virtue mirrors Heaven and Earth is called a "Lord" (*di*). "Lord" and "King" (*wang*) are essentially synonymous titles.
Even if submerged in a great flood that reaches the void, one would not drown.
Jianwu asked Lianshu: "I heard these words from Jieyu: 'Vast and without application; gone and never returning.
I was struck with terror by his words; they were like the Milky Way, boundless and infinite. They were so grand as to be beyond human measure."
[Zhuangzi] was moved by emotion. Lian Shu asked, "What did he say? [Zhuangzi] replied, "On Mount Gushan in the remote distance, there dwells a divine person.
His skin and flesh are like ice and snow; he is as graceful and slender as a young maiden. He does not eat the five grains, but inhales the wind and drinks the dew.
He rides upon the vapors of clouds and drives flying dragons, roaming beyond the four seas. His spirit is so concentrated that it causes all things not to suffer from blight or pestilence."
Yet the years were bountiful and the grain ripened; for this reason, I deceived you and did not believe you. Lian Shu said, "Indeed.
The blind have no means to participate in the viewing of patterns and colors; the deaf have no means to participate in the sounds of bells and drums.
Is it only the physical body that can be deaf or blind? Knowledge, too, can be so. These words of yours are just like those of the woman. Such a person as she—

This is the virtue of such a person. They will embrace the myriad things in their vast expanse, yet they do not seek to bring order to this world. Why should they weary themselves with making the affairs of the world their concern?

Such a person cannot be harmed by anything. Even if a great flood rises up to the heavens, they are not drowned; even in a great drought where metal melts and the earth and mountains wither, they feel no heat.
These [worldly matters] are but the dross and chaff of their being, yet they are still capable of forging and molding the likes of Yao.
"Shun" refers to [the story] from the "Free and Easy Wandering" chapter of the *Zhuangzi*.
Taiyang Wangshou Pingshi had been in Ming'an's quarters for many years; although he had fully grasped the master’s essential teachings, he...
Making his own rise and fall his sole concern, he sought to undermine his colleagues and was jealous of those who excelled him.
At that time, while Langya Guangzhao and Gong’an Yuanjian were living among the assembly, Zen Master Fenyang Shanzhao ordered them to investigate the essential tenets of Ming’an.

Ming’an, the Sun of Taiyang, said, "It is none other than Yuan and Jue who shall cause the school of Dongshan to flourish. The two masters replied, "There is the attendant Ping here. Ming’an said, "That is so."
Pointing his finger at his chest, he said, "This place is not good. Then, pressing his thumb between his crossed fingers, he showed them and said, "Go straight ahead;
you shall die right here. When Ming’an passed away, his final instruction stated: "Bury my body for ten years without difficulty, and then perform a memorial offering for Taeryangsan.
At the time of the interment, his disciples feared that this location might be unfavorable for their master, so they...
The items of yellow and white ware donated by the Commandant Li Hewen were recorded in the inscription on the stupa, yet in reality, they did not exist.
Later, while Píng was residing at Tàiyáng, he suddenly declared, "The geomantic orientation of my late master’s sacred remains is unfavorable; I shall remove them and cremate them.

The senior monks of the monastery earnestly admonished him, but Píng said, "It is an obstacle for me," and proceeded to open the stupa. There, the master’s countenance appeared as if alive, though the firewood had been exhausted.
He stood there solemnly, and the assembly was all struck with wonder. Hui Ping split open [the monk’s] skull with a pickaxe, added more oil and firewood, and in a moment it was reduced to ashes.
The assembly reported this matter to the authorities; Hui Ping was charged for plotting to seize the temple’s property and was forced to return to lay life for his lack of filial piety.
Later, Hui Ping called himself Huang the Scholar and went to visit Langya. Langya said, "The attendant Hui Ping of years past is today the scholar Huang. I..."
While at Taiyang, he saw what you had done and consequently did not accept him. He also visited Gong’an, and Gong’an treated him likewise.
Ping wandered about without support; later, at a three-way intersection, he was devoured by a tiger.
In the end, he could not avoid the prediction of being impaled by the hand-fork of Taiyang. (See *Baohun yinyi*).

"Night after night one embraces the Buddha in sleep," as Master Fu Da Shi’s verse says: "Night after night one embraces the Buddha in sleep; Morning after morning one rises together with him. Whether rising or sitting, we are always in each other's company;
In speech or silence, we dwell together. Not separated by even a hair’s breadth, They are like a body and its shadow. If you wish to know where the Buddha goes,"
"This very sound of speech is it. See the *Zongmen tongyao*, the *Wudeng huiyuan*, and the *Biyue lu*. Regarding the story of Lord Ye painting dragons from the *Zhuangzi*:
Lord Ye was so fond of dragons that he had dragons painted upon his dwellings, curtains, and vessels as objects of play.
Thereupon, the celestial dragon heard this and descended. When Lord Ye saw it, he abandoned his place and fled far away.
People thought that what Lord Ye had cherished was not a true dragon.
Regarding the *Analects*, in the passage where the Master says: "To hear something on the road and repeat it on the road is the abandonment of virtue," the commentary states:
"Even if one hears virtuous words, if one does not take them as one's own, this is to abandon one's own virtue."
"Excellence in the task requires excellence in the tools.
(Analects) Zigong asked about practicing benevolence. The Master said: "A craftsman who wishes to excel in his work must first sharpen his tools."

Regarding the beauty of the music of the *jun* (celestial spheres): Duke Mu of Qin dreamed that he reached the abode of the Emperor, where he beheld the grand music of the *jun-tian*. The Emperor bestowed upon him a decree, and consequently, the state of Qin flourished greatly.
The *Huainanzi* states: "Of the nine heavens, the central one is called *jun-tian*."

The twenty-seventh patriarch, Prajñātāra, did not dwell in the aggregates or realms during his inhalations. Once, while he was being invited for a meal by the King of East India, the king asked, "Everyone here recites the sutras;
why is it that you alone do not? The patriarch replied, "This poor monk’s exhalation does not follow after external conditions."
Inhalation does not abide within the aggregates or elements; one should constantly recite such sutras as these, numbering hundreds of thousands of millions of scrolls, rather than merely one or two.
This is seen in the *Zongmen Tongyao* (Compendium of the Essentials of the School Gate) and the *Canzong Zhengmai* (Orthodox Lineage of the Chan School).
King Śibi, who sacrificed his own flesh for a dove, was one of great diligence. He regarded all sentient beings as his own children. At that time, there was no Buddha in the world.
When Śakra’s life was about to end, he thought to himself, "Where is there a person of omniscience? He questioned everyone everywhere, but none could [satisfy him].
Having his doubts severed, he sat in sorrow. A master of skillful transformations named Viśvakarman asked, "Lord of Devas, why do you grieve?
He replied, "I have sought an omniscient person, yet I have not been able to find one. Viśvakarman said, "There is one of the Kauśika clan, King Śibi;
before long he will become a Buddha. Indra then commanded Viśvakarman to transform himself into a red-eyed pigeon, while he himself transformed into—
A hawk pursued a dove that flew into the king’s armpit seeking refuge. Perched upon a tree, the hawk said to the king, "Return my dove to me.
The king cut flesh from his own thigh and gave it to the hawk. The hawk said, "Though you give me this warm flesh, you must act according to principle so that its weight is equal to that of the dove.
The king placed the scales against the dove; he continued to cut his own flesh until it was entirely exhausted, only then reaching parity with the dove. The Emperor.
The Śākya King said, "When you cut the flesh from your body, was your mind not distressed? The King made this vow: "If I were distressed, my body would not return to its former state;
if I am not distressed, it shall immediately be restored. As soon as he had finished speaking, it was as it was before. (See *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra*, fascicle 4.)
The Buddha said to Śāriputra: "In a past age, there was a brahmin named Nyagrodha. Later, he fathered a son named Mahādatta, whom his father loved dearly.
One day, while out for a stroll, he witnessed various forms of suffering and distress. [He then spoke to...]
His father granted him permission. Of the goods in the treasury, he gave away two-thirds.
Mahādāna (Great Giving), unable to bear the depletion of his father’s wealth, set out upon the sea to gather treasures. Having obtained three pearls, he tied them to the corner of his garment.
When he emerged from the sea and was resting, the nāgas secretly untied and took them away. Upon waking, Mahādāna looked for the pearls and found they were not there; he then...
He reflected, "This must have been taken away by a sea dragon who wishes to drain the great ocean. The sea dragon, knowing this, returned the pearl to him.

Upon returning to his home, he benefited the multitude according to their needs. The details of this account appear in the eighth fascicle of the *Sūtra of the Causes and Conditions of the Wise and the Foolish*.
The *Saptāha-pratyutthita-pāda-bodhisattva-pūrvacaryā-sūtra* states: The Buddha told Ānanda, "I recall that in the distant past, there was a Buddha who appeared in the world named Puṣya.
He had entered meditative absorption within a jeweled cave on the Snowy Mountains. At that time, I went into the mountains to gather medicinal herbs and beheld that Buddha."
His heart was filled with joy; with palms joined and feet raised, he praised that Buddha for seven days and seven nights, thereby transcending nine kalpas.

He then spoke these verses: "In the heavens above and the world below, none is equal to the Buddha... (and so forth). Furthermore, this is seen in the fourth fascicle of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*.
Regarding the Elder Śaṅkara:
In the past, Śākyamuni was a rishi with a conch-shell topknot named Śaṅkara. He constantly sat upright beneath a tree, motionless.
A bird, thinking him to be a piece of wood, laid its eggs upon his topknot. When this Bodhisattva arose from his meditative concentration, he became aware of what was upon his head.
There was a bird’s egg. He reflected to himself: "If I move, the bird will not return, and the egg will surely perish. He immediately returned to meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
Only when the bird had hatched its young and flown away did he arise. (See *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra*, fascicle 17).
The minister Kuvinda divided Jambudvīpa into seven equal portions—cities, towns, mountains, and rivers—so that strife among the various kingdoms would cease. Wisdom.
This is the ultimate point. See the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, fascicle four.

Regarding the resources of the virtuous, the *Daode jing* says: "The virtuous person is the teacher of the non-virtuous; the non-virtuous person is the resource of the virtuous. A refined explanation [of this].

It is said: "A good person can serve as a model for an entire age. Although they differ from those who are not good, if there were no such people in the world who are not good, who would know that a good person is good?
Thus, it is precisely through the existence of the 'not good' that the 'good' serves as a basis [for being known].
A 'basis' (zi) means that one relies upon it to distinguish oneself."

Waving his sleeves and sipping dregs, Qu Yuan had been exiled. He wandered by the marshes of the Yangtze River, walking and chanting along the banks of the wetlands. His complexion was haggard and his appearance withered and emaciated.
A fisherman saw him and asked, "Are you not the Grand Master of Sanlu? For what reason have you come to such a state? Qu [Yuan]—
The Original [Text] says: "The people of the world are all turbid, while I alone am clear; the multitude are all intoxicated, while I alone am sober.
For this reason, I have been cast out. The Fisherman said: "A sage is not obstructed by external things, but is able to move with the times. When the people of the world are all turbid,"
"Why not dig up the mud and splash the waves? When all the people are drunk, why not eat their dregs and drink their lees?

Why do you contemplate so deeply and rise so high, only to let yourself go? Qu Yuan replied, "I have heard that one who has just washed his hair must dust off his cap, and one who has just bathed must shake out his robes. How can I allow my pure body to be defiled by the world's filth?"
"How clouded you are! It would have been better to have leaped into the stream of the Xiang and been buried within the belly of a river fish.
How could one allow such pure whiteness to be defiled by the dust and grime of the mundane world? The fisherman smiled gently, struck his oars, and departed.
He then sang: "The waters of Canglang are clear; therein I may wash my collar-strings. The waters of Canglang are turbid; therein I may wash my feet."
He washed my feet and then departed, no longer engaging me in conversation. Upon reading the *Li sao jing* (Encountering Sorrow) and the *Zhanguo ce* (Strategies of the Warring States),

[I saw that] the seventh fascicle of the *Fahua Dacheng Yinyi* (Phonetic Explanations of the Mahāyāna Lotus Sūtra) contains the characters "baoju" (bundles of gifts) and "angzang" (filthy and unclean).

*Bāojū* (baoju): To wrap up extraordinary objects and present them as offerings out of flattery and sycophancy, seeking to solicit favors or recommendations. *Āngzàng*: The appearance of a body coiled and winding. As the *Hànshū* says:
"With curved brows and an *āngzàng* [posture], leaning against the side of the gate. This is found in the *Yìyì* (Phonetics and Meanings) of the *Bǎoxùn*.

Regarding "shrugging one's shoulders and smiling sycophantically," Zengzi said: "Shrugging one's shoulders and smiling sycophantically is as exhausting as working in the summer vegetable plots. The commentary states: "Shrugging one's shoulders" means tensing the body; "smiling sycophantically" means forcing a smile.
Both are the demeaning manners of a petty person who fawns. "Exhausting" (bing) means labor. "Summer plots" refers to those who tend the vegetable beds during the summer months.
[This] is from the *Mencius*. [The passage continues:
"He does not enter my chamber.
Confucius said: "If someone passes by my gate but does not enter my chamber, the only one for whom I feel no regret is the 'village original' (*xiàngyuán*)."
"Indeed! The 'village original' (xiāngyuán) is a thief of virtue. Upon seeing this passage from Mencius, some said, "In your youth, you were fond of *fu* (rhymeprose).
He replied, "Yes; as a child, I practiced the carving of insects and the engraving of seals. A short while later, he said, "When one is grown..."
"Indeed, it is not for the sake of [mere] action. This is from the "Wenzi" chapter of Yangzi’s *Fayan*.

Regarding the "Meeting Friends through Literature," the *Lunyu* records that Master Zeng said: "The gentleman meets with friends through literature, and through friendship he assists in the cultivation of benevolence (*ren*)."

Regarding the *Analects* passage, "Those of differing paths do not plot together," the Master said: "When paths differ, they do not plot together. The commentary states: "Differing" refers to categories such as good and evil, or the heterodox and the orthodox.
In the *Analects*, it says:
"It takes flight at the sight of color; it circles before it settles. The commentary states: This means that when a bird perceives that a person's countenance is not benevolent, it flies away;
only after circling and observing closely does it descend to rest. This describes how a person perceives the subtle signs (*ji*) and acts, exercising careful discernment.
One’s current situation should also be understood in this way.

Regarding the "Thorn of Sangjian," in the *Liezi*, it is told that after Qiu Hu had married his wife for five days, he departed to serve in Chen. It was only after five years that he returned. As he was about to reach home, he saw—
A woman was gathering mulberry leaves on a path. Her appearance was exceedingly beautiful. A Hu man teased her, saying: "Toiling in the fields is not as good as meeting a young man;
gathering mulberries is not as good as meeting a noble lord. I have gold, which I wish to give to you. The woman would not accept it.
When Hu arrived home and saw his mother, his mother called his wife out; it was the woman from the mulberry grove.

The wife reproached him, saying, "To see a beautiful woman and abandon gold while forgetting your mother is the height of unfiliality. You may marry another as you wish," whereupon she threw herself into the water and died.
A later scholar composed a poem on this, saying: "The husband’s favor is as thin as a leaf, while the wife remains as clear as ice. The husband offers her gold, but the wife does not accept it.

Even if they were to happen upon a single shared smile, who would believe that for half a lifetime she has kept watch by a solitary lamp? The details of this account may also be found in the *Lieguo zhi*.
"Not seeing that which is desirable":
The *Dàodé jīng* says, "Not seeing that which is desirable causes the mind not to be disturbed. The *Jīngjiě* (Precise Explanation) says:
"I do not show people forms that are desirable, so that the minds of the people may naturally become settled and undisturbed."
The character 檃 (yǐn) [composed of 隱 minus 工 and 木] is used to rectify the *Xúnzǐ*.
Those who use wooden braces must employ the *yǐngkuò* (檃括). That which bends the crooked is called *yǐn*; that which makes it square is called *kuò*.
Furthermore, the sides of the *yǐngkuò* often contain curved wood; it is also written as 檃括. The *Shàngshū* mentions the implement of the *yǐngkuò*, which is precisely this.
"It is an instrument of perversity and crookedness.

"Virtue is never solitary," says the *Analects*. The Master said: "Virtue is never solitary; it must have its neighbor. The commentary states: "Neighbor" (*lin*) means "intimate associate. Virtue does not exist in isolation.
Necessity responds according to kind. Therefore, those who possess virtue will surely have their kind follow them, just as a dwelling has its neighbors.

Grasping the six dragons to symbolize Qian (the Hexagram Heaven) in the *Zhouyi*, one greatly illumines the end and the beginning; the six positions are established according to the time. One mounts the six dragons at the proper time to govern Heaven. The commentary states: "This..."
When it is said that the Sage clearly illuminates the beginning and end of the Way of Qian, one sees the six positions of the hexagram, each perfected according to its time;
thus, he mounts these six yang lines to carry out the Way of Heaven—this is the Sage’s ultimate success (yuan-heng).
In the seventh year of the Shenji era, Emperor Guangwu of the Han was born;
a crimson light illuminated his chamber, its reflection resembling that of five qilin and seven phoenixes. A diviner, observing the atmosphere over the city walls of Chongling, said:
"How magnificent! It is lush and verdant. Yu Yingqiu remarked: "He shall bear the phoenix-patterned throne backrest, facing the south as sovereign."

Having ascended the throne of the Great Treasure, he governed the realm from his imperial palace; meeting with this auspicious era, he examined the records of former precedents. "The Emperor’s mind holds him in high regard" (*Lunyu*).

"The Emperor’s ministers are not obstructed; they are held in high regard by the Emperor’s mind. The commentary states: "This quotes the words of the *Tang Gao* (The Announcement of Tang) from the *Shang Shu* (Book of Shang)."
"Jian" means to examine. It states that as for the crimes of Jie, I dare not pardon them; and as for the worthy men of the world, who are all ministers of the Supreme Lord, I dare not conceal them.
They are examined within the heart of the Lord; it is according to what the Lord ordains.

Regarding the labor of mending the dragon-robe, the *Shi* says: "The office of the dragon-robe has a deficiency; it is Zhong Shanfu who mends it. The commentary states: "The 'office of the dragon-robe' refers to the office of the King.

Since the Son of Heaven wears the dragon-robe (*long-gǔn*), one does not dare to speak directly of the King's deficiencies; thus it is said, 'the office of the dragon-robe has a deficiency. This applies even to the King's office."
There were deficiencies and lapses; yet it was only Zhong Shanfu who was uniquely able to remedy them.

Indeed, it is only after one has become a great man that one can rectify the errors in the ruler’s mind. There has never been anyone who, unable to uphold their own virtue, could remedy the deficiencies of their ruler.
This appears in the "Dang" chapter of the *Da Ya* (Greater Odes).

Regarding the image of the hidden dragon in the *Zhou Yi*: "Qian 1: The hidden dragon; do not act. Qian 2: The dragon appears in the field; it is advantageous to see the great man. The commentary states:

"Qian" means to hide. A "dragon" is a yang creature. At the beginning, the yang energy is below; it is not yet fit for application. Therefore, its image is that of a hidden dragon, and its divination says:
"Do not employ. As for the second nine: it is strong, vigorous, central, and correct. It has emerged from hiding and left its seclusion, so its benefits reach all things.
It is what all things benefit from seeing; therefore, its image is "the dragon appearing in the field. Its divination is "it is advantageous to see the great man.
Although the second nine has not yet attained its proper position, the virtue of the great man is already manifest. Ordinary people are insufficient to match it;
thus, this refers to a great man who remains in a subordinate position.
"What closes and brings about the darkness?"—these four lines are from the "Tianwen" (Questions of Heaven) chapter in the fourth volume of Qu Yuan’s *Chuci*.

The subsequent passage, "Entering and exiting heaven and earth while feeling one's way with a single hand," is from Zhou Gongchen’s separate commentary on the *Xunli*. This book [contains]... (Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly; the translation reflects the available portion.)
It consists of nineteen fascicles and is widely circulated in the world.
Tu Nan said: "In the Nine-Ten-Thousand-Li Southern Sea there is a fish; its name is Kun. As for the size of the Kun, one does not know how many thousands of li it measures. It transforms and—"
There is a bird named Peng. One cannot know how many thousands of li its back spans. When it flies in a rage, its wings are like clouds hanging from the sky.
This bird, when the seas are in motion, intends to migrate to the Southern Ocean. As for this Southern Ocean:
It is a celestial pool. The *Qixie* (Harmonious Records) is a book that records the strange. The words of the *Harmonious Records* say:

"When the Peng bird migrates to the Southern Abyss, it strikes the water with its wings for three thousand li. It soars upon the whirlwind of the *fushao*, ascending ninety thousand li. It departs and rests for six months before breathing again.
[The vapors of] wild horses, the dust and dirt—these are all things that breathe life into one another by means of their breath. As for the azure blue of the heavens..."
Is it that its true color has been lost? Or is it that it has traveled so far that it has reached no ultimate destination? Its looking downward is merely like this.
Furthermore, if the accumulation of water is not deep, it lacks the power to support a great ship.
If one pours a cup of water onto a depression in the floor, a mustard seed may serve as a boat; yet if a cup is placed there, it will stick fast. When the water is shallow, the boat...
It is great. If the accumulation of wind is not thick, it will lack the power to support great wings.
Therefore, at ninety thousand li, the wind rises up from below; only then can one gather the wind. With the blue sky upon one's back, unimpeded by anything, only then can one plan to head south.
Excerpted from the "Free and Easy Wandering" chapter of the *Zhuangzi*.
Regarding the "South Pointer":

The people of Yuechang came to present tribute, but upon their return they forgot the way home. The Duke of Zhou fashioned a south-pointing chariot, carving a wooden figure that raised its hand pointing toward the south;
by having them drive it while looking toward the south, they would know the path back home. This is what the modern compass is. See the *Liezi*.
The National Records, along with ancient and modern commentaries, relate that the Buddha, observing a plowman, grew weary of the floating world and addressed the bhikṣus.
When the Bodhisattva had gradually grown older, he went out of the city to travel and observe; having traveled to a garden, he saw...
Seeing the various farmers diligently performing their labors, the Bodhisattva gave rise to compassion in his heart and lamented that the world was subject to such suffering.

Thereupon, beneath a Jambu tree, he contemplated the Dharma for transcending suffering. This is further recorded in the fourth fascicle of the *Vaipulya-purṇabhadra-alaṃkāra-sūtra* (大方廣莊嚴經) and also appears in the *Lalitavistara-sūtra* (普曜經).
Tiwai received the precepts upon beholding the golden man.
Tiwai, together with five hundred merchants, prepared a mixture of parched grain flour and honey beneath a tree and prostrated themselves before the Buddha.

The Buddha reflected that according to the practice of previous Buddhas receiving offerings, they always carried alms bowls; it was not appropriate for him to accept food directly from the hands of others as other practitioners do. At that time, the Four Heavenly Kings...

Each offered a single bowl. The Buddha caused them to be joined together into one bowl. He then accepted the parched flour and honey from the merchant with that bowl and bestowed upon him the prediction of his future Buddhahood, naming him the Tathāgata Madhuvipaśyin (蜜成如來).
This is recorded in the seventh fascicle of the *Puyao jing* (Sutra of Universal Radiance); further details may be found in the *Tiwai jing* (Sutra of Trapusa and Bhallika).

Bian He of Chu cut open the raw jade to reveal the gem. While wandering the Jing Mountains, he found a piece of raw jade and presented it to King Wu. The king sent a jade-cutter to examine it, who declared, "It is stone.
The king, deeming Bian He a fraud, had his left foot amputated. After King Wu died, his son King Wen ascended the throne, and Bian He once again...
He presented it to the King. The King again ordered a jade-carver to examine it, who declared, "It is stone. Furthermore, suspecting Bo He of deception, the King had his right foot amputated.
After King Wen died and his son, King Cheng, ascended the throne, Bo He wished to present the jade once more;

fearing that he might lose his life, he went to the foot of Mount Jing, where he cradled the raw jade in his arms and wept for three days and three nights until his tears were exhausted and he continued with blood. When the King heard of this, he sent a messenger...
A questioner asked, "There are many in the world who have had their feet amputated; why do you grieve so excessively for this one? Yan He replied, "I do not grieve for the amputation itself.
I grieve that a precious jade was labeled as stone, and a man of integrity was named a deceiver; it is for this reason that I grieve.
He followed the messenger's instructions to present it to the King, who ordered a jade-carver to polish it. Indeed, they obtained beautiful jade. The King said, "The two former [assessors]..."
The Lord found it easy to cut off a man’s feet, yet difficult to cleave his stone; thus it was named the "Jade of Mr. He. A later worthy wrote a poem:

"Embracing the stone before the crag, cassia leaves grow thick; The clear stream flows through the ravine as it has for all time. In the empty mountains, as the sun sets, the cries of monkeys resound."
"I suspect it is the people of Jing whose weeping has not yet ceased. (From the *Shiji* and the *Lieguo zhi*).
"Meeting the source on every side" (*Mengzi*):
"The gentleman seeks profound advancement through the Way, desiring that he attain it for himself. When he attains it for himself, then..."
"Abide in it securely. Abide in it securely, and then you will have a deep foundation. With a deep foundation, you will find the source at every turn, whether moving left or right.
Therefore, the gentleman desires that he attain this for himself. The commentary states: "Zào (造)" means to reach or arrive at.

"To reach a profound depth" implies advancing without ceasing. "Dào (道)" refers to the method by which one advances. "Zī (資)" is equivalent to relying upon or drawing from. "Left and right" refers to one's person.

The phrase "on both sides" indicates that [the source] is extremely near yet not in a single location. "Feng" (逢) means to encounter or meet. "Yuan" (原) means the origin; it is the place from which the water comes.

This states that the gentleman must strive for profound cultivation and do so necessarily by means of the Way, desiring that he have something to hold onto and follow, thereby awaiting a silent realization and mental penetration until he naturally attains it within himself. To attain it spontaneously—

Once one has established this, the means by which one abides in it will be secure and firm, unwavering. When one’s abiding is secure and firm, that upon which one relies will be profound and inexhaustible.
When what one relies upon is deep, then in the midst of daily life, one draws from what is most immediate;
there is nowhere one goes without encountering the very foundation of one's resources. See the "Li Lou" chapter of Mencius.
The realization of cultivation was not absent in the Zen Master Nanyue Huairang. He went to Caoxi to attend upon the Sixth Patriarch. The Patriarch asked, "Where have you come from?
The Master replied, "From Mount Song. The Patriarch asked, "What kind of thing comes in such a manner? The Master was speechless. Thus he remained for eight years, until suddenly—
Xuefeng said to National Teacher Baizhang, "I have a point of realization. The Master asked, "How so? Xuefeng replied, "If one describes it as a thing, it is not correct.
The Master asked, "Is there still any need for cultivation and realization? Xuefeng replied, "Cultivation and realization are not non-existent; however, one must not be defiled by them.
The Master said, "This very state of being undefiled is that which all Buddhas protect and keep in mind. Since you are thus," he concluded.
I am also like this. I have brought forth the *Dharma-treasure Platform Sūtra*, as well as the *True Lineage of Chan Meditation* and other works.
It is like when the father composed [the text] and the son recorded the *Zhongyong*. The Master said: "Only King Wen may be called free from sorrow; he had King Ji as his father and King Wu..."
As for a son, he carries on what his father has begun.
*Fahua Dacheng Yinyi*, Scroll Eight: Broadly Bestowing and Relieving the Multitudes.
In the *Analects*, Zigong said: "If there were one who could bestow bounty extensively upon the people and be able to rescue the multitude—how would such a person be?
Could he be called benevolent? The Master said: "What need is there to speak of benevolence? He must surely be a sage! Even Yao and Shun found it difficult to achieve this."
A city of ten thousand households is not easily exchanged for a foot-long jade disc;
such was the case with the Bian He Jade Disc possessed by the state of Zhao. King Zhao of Qin wished to trade fifteen cities of ten thousand households for it.
Zhao sent the Minister Xiangru to deliver it to Qin. Upon arrival, Xiangru observed that King Zhao possessed only a desire to covet the jade disc, yet had no intention of ceding the cities.
He then feigned this, saying, "The jade disc has a flaw; please let me point it out. The King handed the disc to Xiangru.

Xiangru held the disc, leaned against a pillar, and stood there with his hair bristling in anger as it rose above his cap. He then said, "I have heard that even among commoners who meet as friends, they cannot bear to deceive one another."
"How much more so for a great kingdom! If Your Majesty were to harm me, my head and the jade璧 would both shatter against this pillar.

Fearing that the璧 might be destroyed, the King had someone support Xiangru and raise him up, whereupon he returned to Zhao. A later poem by a worthy man says: 'The Bian jade is flawless, its brilliance outshining the sun;
though the King of Qin cherished it, he did not expose his stratagem. How pitiful it was as it fell again into the hands of Xiangru—a single gust of pure wind fills [the world].'"
He returned home by way of the road; the details may be found in the *Shiji* and the *Bingli guozhi*.
Regarding Guan Chuang Caoting Luying:
Zhou Dunyi, styled Maoshu, was a native of Chongling. At that time, the Buddhist monk Foyin was residing at Luanchi. The Master went to pay him a visit, and they conversed together.

While he was lecturing on the Way, [Wang] asked: "The *Doctrine of the Mean* states: 'That which Heaven mandates is called nature; following nature is called the Way. In the Chan gate, why is it said that 'no-mind is the Way'? The Master said:
"If you have doubts, you must study elsewhere. [Wang] said: "There is no doubt that one must study, but ultimately, what constitutes the Way?"
The Master said, "The green mountains fill the eyes; look as you please. Thereupon, the monk attained realization.

One day, seeing weeds growing before the window, he remarked, "This is exactly like my own state of mind. He presented this verse to the Master: "Originally there was no delusion, and now there is no awakening;
Mind and object merge, revealing the hidden depths. Weeds grow deep outside the window, pines stand in the path; All day long they cause people to gaze."
[The Master] did not feel weary. The Master Heshang said: "The substance of the Great Way is vast and all-pervading; why restrict it to the moving and the planted, the flying and the hidden?
Walking, observing, sitting, and contemplating, there is no hindrance at all; to see forms or seek sounds is for the mind itself to feel weary. This is recorded in the *Jianzheng Wenlu*, Volume Nine.
Zhou Maoshu did not remove the weeds before his window. When asked about this, he said, "They share the same essence as my own mind.
Zhang Zithou likewise listened to the braying of a donkey and considered it the same. This is recorded in the *Complete Works of the Two Chengs*.
When Shi Le wished to resist Liu Yao, his ministers and aides all offered counsel against it. He consulted Fo Tucheng, who said, "The wind-bells atop the stupa say:
'Xiuzhi tilegang, Pugu qutudang. This is the language of the Qiang (Jie). 'Xiuzhi' means army; 'tile'..."
*Lìgāng* (戾岡) means "to go forth. *Púgǔ* (僕谷) is the title of Liu Yao as a Hu ruler. *Qútùdāng* (劬禿當) means "to seize. This refers to the military expedition that captured Liu Yao.

Subsequently, Liu Yao was indeed captured. The details may be found in the *Biographies of Eminent Monks* (*Gaoseng zhuan*), the *Biographies of Divine Monks* (*Shenseng zhuan*), and various fragments of sutras and treatises.
The four *caidai* (fast) days are the first day of the month, the full moon, the eighth, and the twenty-third; these are called the four *caidai* days, as seen in the *Baizhang Qinggui*.

Furthermore, it says: "The eighth and fifteenth days of the waxing moon (*baimue*), and the eighth, fourteenth, or fifteenth days of the waning moon (*heimue*)," as seen in the *Fashu* (Dharma Numbers).

When Chan Master Baizhang of Panshan was visiting the market, he saw a guest buying pork and said to the butcher, "Cut me a pound of the finest meat. The butcher set down his knife, folded his hands, and said, "Prefectural Secretary. Baizhang saw through him and recognized him as a successor of Mazu.
Thus it was that while walking through the marketplace, he encountered this incident. The butcher, having laid down his blade, stood with palms joined and addressed him as "Prefectural Secretary."
"That one is not the essence. At these words, the Master attained realization. He then read the *Zongmen Tongyao*, the *Canzong Zhengmai*, and the *Zhuyuelu*.
When Louzi heard lewd words...

Master Louzi’s dharma lineage is not clearly known. One day, while wandering through the streets and markets, he was tying his socks and sash beneath a wine tavern when he heard a song being sung from above:
"Since you have no heart, I shall also cease. At this, he suddenly attained great enlightenment and was thus named Louzi.
This is recorded in the *Zhengmai of the Chan School* and the *Record of Pointing at the Moon*.
Regarding the *sthūlātyaya* offense, the *Sifen lü shanjian ji* states: "Sthūla means 'great obstruction. It refers to obstructing the path of goodness and subsequently falling into the evil realms.
Its essence is base and evil. As for its name being established based on its unwholesome nature, it is because it constitutes the offenses of the first two categories."
In the *Analects*, Confucius expresses his readiness to die at evening;
the Master says, "If one hears the Way in the morning, it is acceptable to die at evening. The commentary states: "The Way is the principle of what is naturally so regarding all things and affairs.

If one truly succeeds in hearing it, then life will be lived in accordance with it and death will be met with peace, leaving no further regrets. This is why [the Master speaks of] morning and evening with such intensity.
Regarding the proximity of that time, Chengzi said: "One must not fail to know the Way (Dao). If one can hear the Way, even death is acceptable.
Yang Xiong did not envy long life.
Someone asked Yangzi: "People envy long life, doing so for the sake of learning. Can this be called a love of learning? Yangzi said: "This is not yet a love of it.
[The] commentary states: "Zhongni was intent on the Way; he would have died in the evening had he heard it in the morning. Yangzi loved learning; he did not envy long life.
This is from the "Xue Xing" (Learning and Conduct) chapter of the *Fayan* (The Master’s Words).

At that time, in the city of Kuśinagara, there was the son of an artisan named Cunda. He prostrated before the Buddha and said, "I pray only that the World-Honored One and the community of bhikṣus will accept my final offering. We are impoverished and wish to follow the Tathāgata."
He requested food for the future, saying, "I only pray that you will compassionately accept our humble offering, and then enter *nirvāṇa*. The Buddha said, "Excellent, excellent!
I shall now sever your poverty for you. With the rain of the Unsurpassed Dharma, I shall drench the field of your body, causing you to be fully endowed with the *dānapāramitā*.
Cunda addressed the assembly, saying, "Together let us prostrate and entreat the Buddha not to enter *nirvāṇa*. The Buddha—
He said, "It is the nature of all Buddhas that conditioned phenomena are likewise so; you should quickly prepare what you have offered and it is not fitting to delay long.
At that time, devas and humans all came to present offerings, but the Buddha accepted none of them. The great assembly cried out, "Excellent, Cunda! You have accomplished great merit.
The World-Honored One desires to fulfill the vows of the multitude," and thus the emanated Buddhas from his pores and the community of bhikṣus all accepted the offerings. The world...
The World-Honored One himself partook of what was offered by Cunda. By the Buddha’s supernatural power, all were fully satisfied.
The details of this are found in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*. At that time, the Buddha and Ānanda went to the house of Cunda the smith;
this was the place where the Tathāgata took his final meal. Having received the food, the World-Honored One then spoke these verses: "I now..."
This was his final meal, taken at the home of Cunda. Such a body of the five aggregates shall before long enter parinirvāṇa.
As stated in the *Padmavaktra-sūtra*:
"One shall escape being food for ants."
When Zhuangzi was about to die, his disciples wished to provide him with a lavish burial. Zhuangzi said, "I shall take heaven and earth as my outer and inner coffins;
the sun and moon as my paired jade discs; the stars as my pearls and gems; and the myriad things as my funeral offerings.
Are my burial requisites not complete? What more could be added? The disciples replied, "We fear that crows and vultures will devour you, Master. Zhuangzi—
He said: "If it is above, it will be eaten by crows and hawks; if it is below, it will be eaten by earthworms and ants. To take from those and give to these—how partial this is!
This is from the "Miscellaneous Chapters" of the *Zhuangzi*.
In the past, there was a king named Prasenajit. The king had a crown prince named Sudāṇa (Good Conqueror).

Upon seeing those suffering punishment within the prison, he felt compassion and pity in his heart and petitioned his father for clemency. The ministers would not permit it, and the king, enraged, intended to execute him.
When the Crown Prince’s mother, the Queen, heard this, she addressed the Great King, saying, "I pray that you will grant the Crown Prince permission to practice giving for half a month.

Thereupon, within the Garden of Sunlight (Sūryaprabha), he established a great assembly for almsgiving. At that time, the Tathāgata King Lamp of Space (Gaganapradīparāja), knowing that [the prince] was ready to be delivered, entered the garden to preach the Dharma and caused him to attain the fruits of the Path. This is excerpted from the seventy-third fascicle of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.
The Auspicious Elder, the Buddha, addressed the bhikṣus: "The Bodhisattva reflected: 'Upon what seat did the Buddhas of the past sit when they realized awakening?
While he was reflecting thus, he immediately knew that all the Buddhas of the past sat upon pure grass when they attained perfect enlightenment. He further considered: 'Who [provided this]...'"

When he was able to provide such pure grass for me, Śakra-devānām-indra immediately transformed his body into that of a grass-cutter and stood to the right of the Bodhisattva, holding the grass. The Bodhisattva asked, "What is your name? He replied, "My name is Śrī.
The Bodhisattva reflected, "I now seek auspiciousness for myself, and I also wish to enable others to obtain it."
Auspicious! A person named Śrī stood before me. I have now definitively realized unexcelled bodhi.
He sat upon pure grass and made this vow: "If I do not realize the unsurpassed, great bodhi in this very life, I would rather let this body be shattered;
I shall never rise from this seat. (From the *Lalitavistara Sūtra*, Scroll Eight).
*Fahua Dacheng Yinyi*, Scroll Nine. Regarding "The Two Nans, Ya, and Songs":
