"The Two Nans" refers to the *Zhou Nan* and *Shao Nan*, which are titles of sections in the *Shijing*. "Ya" refers to the *Daya* and *Xiaoya*. "Songs" [refers to the *Songs*].
These refer to the *Zhou Song*, *Lu Song*, and *Shang Song* [sections] of the *Book of Odes*. For details, see the *Xiaozhu* (Minor Commentary) on the *Book of Odes*.
Regarding the "Songs of Spring and Snow," King Xiang of Chu asked Song Yu: "Master, do you perhaps have some lingering faults? Why is it that the officials, the common people, and the masses..."
This was an extreme form of praise. Song Yu replied, "Yes, indeed it is so. I pray that Your Majesty will show leniency toward my offense and allow me to finish my speech.
There was once a guest who sang in the capital of Ying. At first, he sang the pieces "Xia" and "Li Baren," and those in the state who joined in the chorus numbered several thousand.
When he sang "Yang A" and "Xie Lu," those in the state who joined in the chorus numbered only several hundred.
As for the person [who sings] "Yangchun Baixue" (The Spring Breeze and the Snow), there were only several dozen people in the kingdom who joined in harmony with it.
When the notes of Shang were drawn out and Yu was struck, interspersed with the flowing Zhi, those in the kingdom who could join in harmony did not exceed a few individuals.
Thus, the more lofty the melody, the fewer those who can harmonize with it (and so forth). This is seen in detail in the *Zhan Guo Ce* (Strategies of the Warring States).

In the thirteenth year of the Zhenguan era, after Dharma Master Lin had been called by name for seven days, the court sorcerer Qin Shiying slandered him, claiming that Master Huilin had authored a treatise insulting the imperial lineage.

An edict was issued to arrest Lin; becoming aware of this, Lin changed his attire and voluntarily bound himself, presenting himself at the palace gate to request punishment. The Imperial Decree stated: "Based on..."

"According to your argument, those who recollect Avalokiteśvara are not harmed even when facing execution. Now, having examined the nature of my crime, I am due to be sentenced to death by dismemberment.
I request a seven-day reprieve so that you may diligently recite his name for me, so that I might be spared from execution. However, upon receiving the imperial decree, I did not recite it at all."

When the appointed time arrived, the Emperor issued an edict inquiring, "How has your recitation of Avalokiteśvara been answered by response? He replied, "At the end of the Sui dynasty, the ruler lost his virtue and the four seas were in turmoil.
Your Majesty has cleared the realm and brought your Way to all living beings. Since seven days ago, I have not recited the name of Avalokiteśvara;
I have only recited the name of Your Majesty. The Emperor marveled at these words and dispatched the Censor Wei Cong to inquire of Ling about the reason for his recitation.

When asked about his appearance, he replied: "Avalokiteśvara is the Most Holy One; manifesting forms within the six realms, from the heavens above to the earth below, he serves as a teacher and savior for all.
Your Majesty presides over the imperial throne, and the myriad nations rejoice in your heart. Your civil governance is upright and peaceful, and your spiritual discernment reaches beyond all bounds.

Your holiness is equal to that of Avalokiteśvara; therefore, I think only of Your Majesty... (and so forth). Emperor Zong reported these words to the throne, and by imperial decree, [the monk] was exempted from [further service].
He was sentenced to penal servitude in Yizhou. Master [Hui]shi authored the *Bianzheng lun* (Treatise on Distinguishing Orthodoxy) in eight fascicles and died at Bailao Pass in Shu.
Not long after, Qin Shiying was executed. This is recorded in the *Fozu tongzai*.
Sūn Jìngdé Recites the Sutra One Thousand Times during the Tiānpíng Era of the Wèi Dynasty.
During the Tiānpíng era of the Wèi dynasty, Sūn Jìngdé of Dìngzhōu fashioned an image of Avalokiteśvara and constantly paid it worship. Later, he was attacked by bandits;
unable to endure the torture and interrogation, he falsely confessed to the crime. As he was about to be executed, he dreamed of a śramaṇa who...

He recited the *Sūtra on Avalokiteśvara Saving Life* one thousand times and was thus delivered from his peril. While being led to the marketplace by the officials who had bound him, he continued to recite as he walked;

when he reached the place of execution, having completed the full thousand recitations, the executioner’s blade shattered into three pieces. His skin and flesh remained unharmed. This occurred three times in succession, and each time the blade broke as before.
The officials were struck with wonder and reported the matter in detail to the Chancellor Gao Huan, petitioning for his life to be spared. An imperial edict was issued.
He transcribed this sutra and widely disseminated it throughout the world. When Sun Jingde returned home, he saw three knife-marks upon the neck of the image.
Such was its spiritual resonance. This is recorded in volume seventeen of the Fayuan zhulin (Forest of Gems in the Garden of the Dharma).
Daojiong resided at Nanjian Temple in the capital of the Song dynasty. Daojiong’s secular surname was Ma, and he was a native of Fufeng. He left the household life as a disciple of Daoyi.
When Daoyi fell ill, he once dispatched Daojiong and three others—four people in total—to Mount Huo in Henan to collect stalactites. They entered a cave.
After traveling several li, they crossed a stream by means of a wooden bridge; three men drowned and their torches were extinguished as well. Xiong realized there was no way to escape.
Having long recited the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and maintained mindfulness of Avalokiteśvara, he saw a flash of fire and was thus able to emerge from the cave.
(See the *Fayuan zhulin* and the *Biographies of Eminent Monks*).
The Great Amnesty of the State of Lu.

In the twenty-second year of Duke Zhuang of Lu, in the first month of spring, under the [reigning] King, a great amnesty was proclaimed. The commentary states: "Si" means to release; "sheng" means transgression.

To release and pardon great transgressions is like the modern-day imperial pardon (shu); it means that those with the greatest crimes are all granted clemency. This is specifically recorded in the *Chunqiu*.

The bookshop has committed a great error. Amidst the mourning and burial for Wenjiang, we have produced the sixth volume of the *Spring and Autumn Annals* (Chunqiu), containing the annotated commentary and critical analysis of the *Zhuang Gong* section, which praises his ability to rectify his transgressions.

During the Tang dynasty, Emperor Taizong prohibited flogging on the backs. Having read the *Mingtang Needling and Moxibustion Treatise*, he noted that it states: "The connections of the five viscera are all attached to the back. He issued an edict stating:
"From now on, no prisoner shall be flogged on the back. This is recorded in the *Jian Shu* (Book of Mirrors) and the *Tang Shi* (History of the Tang).

"There are three acts of unfiliality," said Mencius, "and of these, lacking posterity is the greatest. The commentary states: "According to the rites, there are three matters that constitute unfiliality:

first, to flatter one's will and yield to it in a crooked manner, thereby leading one's parents into unrighteousness; second, when the family is poor and the parents are old, to fail to seek official service for their sake."
"Second, not marrying so as to remain childless and sever the ancestral sacrifices. Third. Among these three, the lack of descendants is the greatest offense.
This is from Mencius, Chapter Li Lou.
Upon arriving at the scene, Chan Master Deng Yinpeng took his leave of Mazu one day. Mazu said, "Where are you going? The Master replied, "To Shitou.
Mazu said, "The path to Shitou is slippery. The Master said, "Carrying my staff and wood with me, I perform my play wherever the stage appears," and he departed. As soon as he arrived...
Shitou then circumambulated the meditation seat once, struck his staff once, and asked, "What is the essential principle? Shitou replied, "Heaven! Heaven! The Master was speechless.
He returned and reported this to Mazu. Mazu said, "Go back to him again; when he says 'Heaven! Heaven!', you should then blow twice.
The Master went back and followed the previous instructions in asking the question. Shitou then blew twice.
The Master remained silent once more. Upon returning, he recounted this to Mazu, who said, "I told you that the path at Shitou is slippery.
(From *Chongyao of the Chan School*, *Wudeng Huiyuan*, and *Zhuyue Lu*).
Regarding "Going to Another Country Without Companions," the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: The Buddha told the bhikṣus, "In a past age, there was a country named Vārāṇasī.
At that time, there was a great and filial Brahmin named Bhāradvāja who served as the royal preceptor and constantly instructed five hundred disciples. At that time...
O Brahmin, there was a slave named Karaka who, having heard the sound of the Dharma being preached, was able to retain it all in his memory.
Once, while harboring a slight resentment toward some young boys, he went to another country and falsely claimed, "I am the son of the Ruci Brahmin.
The royal preceptor was greatly delighted and said to him, "I have a daughter whom I shall now give to you as a wife. He replied, "I accept."

[He] taught him. That man was constantly angry regarding food and drink. His wife thought to herself, "If someone should happen to come from the kingdom of Vārāṇasī, I shall receive instruction from him.
When that brāhmaṇa heard this matter in its entirety, he departed for another country.

The man prostrated himself and said, "I have come to this country and claim to be the son of the Great Master; I hope you, my lord, will not disclose this matter. The master said, "You are truly my..."

The son immediately returned home with his master and said, "I have come personally to prepare food and drink for you. His wife then asked the brahmin in secret, "My husband’s meals are always unsatisfactory;
I pray that the Honored One will instruct me. The guest replied, "When I am about to depart, I shall teach you a verse.

The man was seeking a companion, so his wife requested the verse. The guest taught her the verse, saying: "Even if one eats the finest delicacies, If the mind is not at ease, it is as if one has eaten nothing. But if one eats even coarse food with a joyful heart, One will find satisfaction and nourishment."
"Having no kin, he went to another country and deceived the people of the world. Coarse food was his constant meal; why then should he have disliked fine food?
His wife reflected on this verse, and because that man always spoke with gentle words, she no longer gave rise to anger.
The Buddha said: "That brahmin was I myself; that slave was the bhikṣu Chanda."
The King asked for *saindhava*, O son of good family. The secret language of the Tathāgata is extremely profound and difficult to understand.
It is like a great king who tells his ministers, "Bring *saindhava*. Now, *saindhava* has four meanings: first, salt; second, a vessel; third, water; [and fourth, a horse].
Fourth, there are four such qualities of a horse that share this same name: "the wise minister. One who is skilled in knowing these names acts as follows:
when the king is bathing and requests *saindhava*, he immediately offers water; when the king is eating and requests *saindhava*, he immediately offers salt;
and when the king has finished eating and wishes to drink a beverage, requesting *saindhava*, he immediately offers a vessel. If...

When the king wished to go on a journey, he requested *siddhārtha*. [The minister] immediately presented him with a horse. In this way, the wise minister skillfully understood the four kinds of secret speech of the Great King.
The Mahāyāna sūtras are also like this. [This passage] is from the tenth fascicle of the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*.

Regarding "the chariots and horses were packed shoulder-to-shoulder" from Zuo Si’s *Fu*: "The chariots and horses thundered and startled; *hōng-hōng* and *tián-tián*. The *Shiji* states: "*Tián-tián* refers to a great multitude, as it does today in the term *piántián*;
it is also the sound of a crowd moving together."
The mind was deluded regarding the Lotus Sūtra.
Dharma Master Fada of Hongzhou had recited the Lotus Sūtra three thousand times.

Later, he prostrated before the Sixth Patriarch and said, "I only pray that the Master, out of great compassion, will briefly explain the principles and meanings within this sūtra. The Patriarch asked, "In reciting this sūtra, what do you take as its central essence?"
The Master said, "I am a dull-witted student. From the beginning, I have merely recited this according to the text; how could I have known its fundamental principle?
The Patriarch said, "Try reciting it for me once, and I shall explain it for you. The Master then recited it aloud. When they reached the "Chapter on Expedient Means," the Patriarch said, "Stop.
This sutra fundamentally takes the appearance of the world through causes and conditions as its central theme. Although it employs many kinds of parables..."
The parable also does not go beyond this. Why? Because the causal conditions consist solely of one great matter. This one great matter is precisely the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.

You must be careful not to misinterpret the meaning of the sutra. If you see that the "opening, showing, awakening, and entering" belong exclusively to the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, and that we have no share in it—if you interpret it thus, you are slandering the sutra and defaming the Buddha. Since he is already...

The Buddha has already fully realized and perceived this; what need is there to further open it up? You should now believe that the Buddha’s realization and perception is nothing other than your own mind, having no separate essence.

It is simply because all sentient beings obscure their own radiance, greedily clinging to sensory objects, and being disturbed internally by external conditions, that they willingly allow themselves to be driven about.
Thus, I must trouble myself to arise from samādhi and, with various bitter words, urge you toward awakening.
"Rest and sleep; do not seek outside. You are no different from the Buddha; therefore it is said, 'Opening the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.

If you merely toil in clinging to thoughts, claiming them to be your daily practice, how is this any different from a yak that loves its own tail? The Master said, "If that is so, then one need only understand the meaning;
there is no need for the labor of reciting the sutras. The Patriarch said, "What fault is there in the sutras? How could they hinder your mindfulness? It is simply because—"

Delusion and awakening depend on the person; loss and gain arise from yourself. Listen to my verse: "When the mind is deluded, it is turned by the Lotus Sutra; When the mind is awakened, it turns the Lotus Sutra.
If one recites the sutra for a long time without clarity, One becomes an enemy to its true meaning. Without thought, every thought is correct; With thought, every thought becomes deviant.
When neither existence nor non-existence is reckoned, One forever drives the white ox-cart. The Master received this instruction and never ceased his practice.
Recite and uphold it. The details are found in the *Dharma Jewel Platform Sutra*. Now, based on the *Record of the True Lineage of the Chan School*, this has been extracted.
*The Great Achievement of the Lotus Sutra: Phonology and Meaning* (End).

In the past, there was a monk who was reciting the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*. When he reached the verse, "All dharmas from the very beginning / Are eternally of the nature of quiescent extinction," a doubt suddenly arose in his mind that did not cease day or night.
Suddenly, hearing the song of a warbler, he attained sudden enlightenment and continued the preceding verse, saying:
"All dharmas from the very beginning / Are eternally of the nature of quiescent extinction; Spring arrives and the hundred flowers bloom / As the yellow warbler sings among the willows."
[Supplement]. See the *Wudeng huiyuan* and the *Zhuyuelu*.
Dharma Master Sengrui was a native of Changle in Wei Commandery. By the age of eighteen, he had taken Dharma Master Sengxian as his preceptor.

He was extensively learned in the sūtras and śāstras, and his excellent reputation spread far and wide. When Kumārajīva translated the scriptures, Sengrui participated in verifying them alongside him. Master Kumārajīva...

Regarding the translation of the scriptures, in the "Chapter on Receiving the Prediction" (*Vyākaraṇa-parivarta*) of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, it says: "The gods see humans, and humans see the gods.

Daorong remarked, "This phrasing is identical in meaning to that of the Western Regions (India), though the expression is somewhat excessive. Sengrui said, "Could this not mean that humans and devas meet, so that both are able to see one another?
Kumārajīva rejoiced and said, "It is indeed so. That I have been able to encounter you while transmitting and translating these sutras and śāstras leaves me with no regrets whatsoever."
The details may be found in the *Biographies of Eminent Monks* (*Gaoseng zhuan*).

Tang Mingjie, surnamed Yao, was originally a monk of Puguang Temple. He was by nature intelligent and quick-witted, skilled in literary composition, proficient in calligraphy, adept at painting, and capable of playing the qin.
He constantly took pleasure in the mundane world and found no joy in the gates of the Way. In the first year of the Longshuo era, he was nominated...
He responded to the imperial summons and traveled to Luoyang. Upon passing the examinations, he returned to lay life and said, "I have now cast off this donkey skin;

I am already among men. He then prepared wine and gathered various scholars and laypeople, composing a poem that read: "The One Vehicle is fundamentally non-existent; to what can the Three Emptinesses return?
(and so forth). Not long after, he passed away. Later, he appeared in a dream to his acquaintance Zhizheng of Jingtu Temple, saying: "Ming..."

He explained, "In my past lives, I lacked merit and did not follow the inner teachings; thus, I now suffer from hunger and deprivation. If you still have the sentiments of an old friend, could you perhaps grant me a single meal?
Zhizheng granted his permission in a dream. Upon waking, he prepared food for him. Later that night, the spirit came again in a dream to express his gratitude.
This continued until the autumn of the second year, when the spirit again entrusted a message to a painter in a dream, saying: "Because I did not believe in the Buddha-dharma, I am now suffering..."
"Daiku, you must strive for my sake to transcribe two or three fascicles of scripture and recite them eighteen times. Having spoken thus, he composed a poem to part from him:
Holding hands, we cannot part; Pressing my chest, I grieve within. How painful that time’s shadow is short; How tragic that the road to the spring is long.
The pine forest shudders at the wild wind; The desolate earth falls under the cold frost. In bidding farewell, what gift can I give? I leave my heart within.
The regulations state that the painter was originally illiterate; he had others record [the text] for him, and it has been transmitted through both monastics and laypeople in various ways.

This appears in the *Mingbao ji* (Records of Miraculous Retribution), as well as in the *Xu gaoseng zhuan* (Continued Biographies of Eminent Monks) and the *Fayuan zhulin* (Forest of Gems in the Garden of the Dharma).
The *Ekottarika Āgama* states: The Buddha told Ānanda, "Ānanda, strike the *gandī* bell immediately.
Today, the fifteenth day of the seventh month, is the day for the *pravāraṇā* ceremony. Ānanda then ascended the lecture hall, took the *gandī* bell in his hand, and spoke this verse:
"Having subdued the enemy of Māra’s power, having eliminated all fetters without remainder, the *gandī* is struck in the open air; when the bhikṣus hear it, they shall [assemble]."
Gather all those who wish to hear the Dharma to cross the ocean of birth and death. Upon hearing this wondrous sound, let them all assemble here like clouds.

Master Chong said: "In reading the scriptures, one must understand their meaning; understanding the meaning leads to practice. If one studies according to the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*), then..."
Entering the City of Nirvana, if one does not understand the meaning, one will mostly see what is not so, like a blind person who merely seeks out the text and occupies vast ground;
the ox of the mind refuses to plow, and every field is nothing but weeds—where then could the rice grow? (See *Zongjing Lu*).

The Tripitaka Master Yi Jing of the Tang Dynasty composed the following poem titled "Verses on Seeking Scriptures": "Between the Jin, Song, Qi, Liang, and Tang dynasties, Eminent monks left Chang’an to seek the Dharma.
Of those who went, hundreds returned, yet not even ten; How could those who came later have known the hardships faced by their predecessors?"

On the distant road, the azure sky is but a mass of cold; the sands and rivers block the sun, exhausting all strength. If later worthies have not yet mastered this principle, they will often regard the scriptures as something easily understood, merely looking at them for names and meanings.
*Mingyi ji* (Collection of Names and Meanings).
